105082.e: The annular ligament wraps around the head of the radius like a ring. That way the radius can turn inside it without slipping out.
105082.m: A ring ligament holds the head of the radius at the elbow.

105083.q: Which forearm bone turns around the other when you turn your hand over?
105083.e: The ulna stays almost still during the turn. The radius crosses over the ulna and takes the hand with it.
105083.m: When you turn your hand, it is mainly the radius that moves.

105084.q: What other name is used for a pivot joint?
105084.e: Pivot joints are also called wheel joints or trochoid joints, because one part turns like a wheel or around a peg.
105084.m: A pivot joint is also called a wheel joint or trochoid joint.

105085.q: What shape are the joint surfaces of an ellipsoid (egg-shaped) joint?
a: An oval head lies in an oval socket
A ball lies in a round socket
A roller lies in a groove
Two flat discs lie on top of each other
105085.e: The head of the joint is long and oval like an egg and fits into a socket of the same shape. That is where the name comes from.
105085.m: In an ellipsoid joint, an egg-shaped head sits in an oval socket.

105086.q: Around how many axes can an ellipsoid joint move?
105086.e: An ellipsoid joint allows movements around two axes, for example forwards and back and to the side.
105086.m: An ellipsoid joint has two axes of movement.

105087.q: Which joint in the hand is an ellipsoid joint?
a: The joint between the radius and the wrist bones
The joint between the ulna and the upper arm
105087.e: The upper wrist joint connects the radius with the wrist bones. Its joint surfaces are oval.
105087.m: The joint between the radius and the wrist bones is an ellipsoid joint.

105088.q: Which movements does the ellipsoid joint in the wrist allow?
a: Bending and straightening plus tilting to the side
Circling around all axes and rotating
105088.e: You can bend your hand up and down and tilt it towards the thumb or little finger side. Rotating, on the other hand, is not possible in an ellipsoid joint.
105088.m: In the wrist’s ellipsoid joint you can bend, straighten and tilt sideways.

105089.q: Why can’t an ellipsoid joint turn around its own axis?
a: The oval head jams in the oval socket
It has grown together with bone
There are no muscles for it
105089.e: An egg-shaped head only fits into the long socket in one position. If you turn it, it gets stuck.
105089.m: The oval shape stops an ellipsoid joint from rotating.

105090.q: What else is the egg-shaped joint called?
105090.e: An ellipse is an oval. That is why the egg-shaped joint is also called an ellipsoid joint.
105090.m: The egg-shaped joint is also called an ellipsoid joint.

105091.q: Which head movement does the ellipsoid joint between the skull and the first neck vertebra make possible?
105091.e: The upper head joint is an ellipsoid joint. It mainly allows nodding and slight tilting of the head to the side.
105091.m: The ellipsoid joint below the skull allows nodding.

105092.q: What wraps a true joint like a closed tube?
105092.e: The joint capsule surrounds the whole joint and seals the joint space tightly.
105092.m: The joint capsule wraps a true joint like a tube.

105093.q: Which two layers make up the joint capsule?
a: An outer fibrous layer and an inner joint lining
105093.e: The tough outer fibrous layer gives support. The delicate inner layer, the joint lining, lines the inside of the joint.
105093.m: The joint capsule has a tough outer layer and a delicate inner lining.

105094.q: Which layer of the joint capsule makes the joint lubricant?
105094.e: The joint lining, also called the synovial membrane, releases the fluid into the joint space.
105094.m: The joint lining makes the joint lubricant.

105095.q: In medical language, what does the ending “-itis” mean in words such as bronchitis or arthritis?
105095.e: In medicine the ending “-itis” means inflammation. An inflammation of the joint lining, for example, is called synovitis.
105095.m: The ending “-itis” stands for an inflammation.

105096.q: What strengthens the joint capsule from the outside and makes the joint stable?
105096.e: Many ligaments are woven into the joint capsule or lie right against it. They prevent too much movement.
105096.m: Ligaments strengthen the joint capsule from the outside.

105097.q: What is the narrow space between the cartilage surfaces inside the joint capsule called?
105097.e: The joint space is filled with joint fluid. On an X-ray you see it as a dark gap between the bones.
105097.m: The joint space lies between the cartilage surfaces.

105098.q: What do you call connections between bones with no joint space and no joint capsule?
105098.e: In false joints, the bones are joined directly by cartilage or connective tissue, for example at the pubic symphysis. They can hardly move.
105098.m: False joints have no joint space and no capsule.

105099.q: How do you know with your eyes closed whether your arm is bent?
a: Sensors in joints and muscles report it to the brain
105099.e: Tiny sensors for position and movement sit in the joint capsule, ligaments and muscles. They constantly send messages to the brain.
105099.m: Sensors in the joint capsule tell the brain where the joints are.

a: In the joint space between the bones
105100.e: Joint fluid fills the narrow space between the cartilage surfaces of a joint. There it works like a lubricant.
105100.m: The joint fluid is in the joint space.

105101.q: Because of its sticky texture, what substance does joint fluid remind people of?
105101.e: Joint fluid is clear and stringy like egg white. Its technical name, synovia, probably contains the Latin word “ovum” for egg.
105101.m: Joint fluid is sticky and clear like raw egg white.

105103.q: Why is joint fluid vital for the joint cartilage?
a: The cartilage has no blood vessels and is nourished by it
105103.e: Joint cartilage has no blood vessels of its own. It gets nutrients from the joint fluid.
105103.m: Joint cartilage is nourished by the joint fluid.

105104.q: Why is regular exercise good for cartilage?
a: Pressure and release pump nutrients into the cartilage
Exercise makes the joint fluid thinner
105104.e: Cartilage works like a sponge. Under load, fluid is squeezed out; when the load is released, it soaks up fresh joint fluid with nutrients.
105104.m: Exercise pumps nutrients into cartilage like a sponge.

105105.q: What do you call an abnormal build-up of fluid in a joint?
105105.e: After injuries or with inflammation, too much fluid often forms. The joint then swells up and feels tight.
105105.m: A joint effusion is too much fluid in the joint.

105106.q: What is the test called in which joint fluid is taken out with a needle?
105106.e: In an aspiration, the doctor inserts a fine needle into the joint. The fluid is examined, for example for bacteria or blood.
105106.m: In a joint aspiration, joint fluid is taken out with a needle.

105107.q: What does healthy joint fluid look like?
105107.e: Healthy joint fluid is see-through and slightly yellowish. Cloudy or bloody fluid points to inflammation or an injury.
105107.m: Healthy joint fluid is clear and pale yellow.

105108.q: What is a meniscus in the knee made of?
105108.e: Menisci are made of fibrocartilage. It is firm yet elastic and can absorb pressure well.
105108.m: A meniscus is made of elastic fibrocartilage.

105109.q: What does the Greek word “meniscus” mean?
105109.e: The menisci are curved like a half moon. That is why they were given the name “little moon”.
105109.m: Meniscus means “little moon” because it is shaped like a crescent moon.

105110.q: Which meniscus tears much more often?
105110.e: The inner meniscus is attached to the inner ligament and cannot move out of the way as easily. That is why it tears more often.
105110.m: The inner meniscus tears more often than the outer meniscus.

105111.q: During which movement does a meniscus tear especially easily?
a: Twisting on a bent knee that is carrying weight
105111.e: If you twist with your knee bent and your whole weight on it, the meniscus gets trapped between the bones. This often happens in football or skiing.
105111.m: Twisting on a bent knee is dangerous for the meniscus.

105112.q: Which method is usually used today to operate on a torn meniscus?
a: A large cut right across the knee
105112.e: In keyhole surgery, called arthroscopy, a camera and fine instruments are inserted into the knee through small cuts.
105112.m: A torn meniscus is usually operated on with keyhole surgery.

105113.q: Why does a tear in the inner part of the meniscus heal poorly?
a: This part has hardly any blood supply
This part is made of bone
This part has too many nerves
This part lies outside the knee
105113.e: Only the outer edge of the meniscus has blood vessels. The inner area lacks the nutrients needed for healing.
105113.m: The inner part of the meniscus has hardly any blood supply and heals poorly.

105114.q: Between which bones do the menisci lie?
a: Between the thigh bone and the shin bone
Between the kneecap and the fibula
Between the shin bone and the heel bone
Between the hip bone and the thigh bone
105114.e: The menisci sit on top of the shin bone. The rounded ends of the thigh bone roll and glide on them.
105114.m: The menisci lie between the thigh bone and the shin bone.

105115.q: Apart from cushioning, what job do the menisci have?
a: They enlarge the contact area and spread the pressure
105115.e: The rounded ends of the thigh bone do not fit well on the flat shin bone. The menisci fill the gap, so the load is spread over a larger area.
105115.m: Menisci spread the pressure in the knee over a larger area.

105116.q: Which cruciate ligament tears much more often?
105116.e: The anterior (front) cruciate ligament is under heavy strain when you twist or stop suddenly. Tearing it is one of the most common serious knee injuries in sport.
105116.m: The anterior cruciate ligament tears much more often than the posterior one.

105117.q: Which movement does the anterior cruciate ligament prevent?
105117.e: The anterior cruciate ligament runs at an angle from the shin bone backwards and upwards to the thigh bone. This stops the shin bone from sliding forwards.
105117.m: The anterior cruciate ligament stops the lower leg from sliding forwards.

105118.q: How does a doctor check whether the anterior cruciate ligament is torn?
a: She carefully pulls the lower leg forwards
She taps the heel with a hammer
She listens to the knee with a stethoscope
105118.e: If the shin bone can be pulled unusually far forwards, the anterior cruciate ligament is no longer holding. Often an MRI scan is done as well.
105118.m: A loose shin bone shows a torn cruciate ligament.

105119.q: In which sport, popular in Switzerland, are especially many cruciate ligaments torn?
105119.e: When skiing, the skis can twist the knee while the body keeps moving. Football also causes many cruciate ligament tears.
105119.m: Skiing and football are typical sports for cruciate ligament tears.

105120.q: In an operation, what is a torn cruciate ligament often replaced with?
a: A piece of the patient’s own tendon
105120.e: Often a tendon from the thigh or part of the kneecap tendon is used. It is anchored in the knee as a new ligament.
105120.m: A new cruciate ligament is often made from the body’s own tendon.

105121.q: What do people often notice at the moment a cruciate ligament tears?
a: An audible pop in the knee
105121.e: Many people report a bang or pop in the knee. Afterwards the knee usually swells quickly and feels unstable.
105121.m: A cruciate ligament tear is often noticed as a pop in the knee.

105122.q: What helps athletes prevent a cruciate ligament tear?
a: Strong leg muscles and a good warm-up
Only doing sport in the evening
105122.e: Strong thighs and calves support the knee. If you warm up and land jumps cleanly, you twist your knee less often.
105122.m: Strong leg muscles protect the cruciate ligaments.

105123.q: How many cruciate ligaments does a knee joint have?
105123.e: Each knee has an anterior (front) and a posterior (back) cruciate ligament. Together they keep the knee stable forwards and backwards.
105123.m: Each knee has a front and a back cruciate ligament.

105124.q: Unlike a tendon, what does a ligament connect?
105124.e: Ligaments hold bones together at joints. Tendons, on the other hand, pass the force from a muscle to a bone.
105124.m: Ligaments connect bones, tendons connect muscles to bones.

105125.q: What are ligaments mainly made of?
a: Tough connective tissue with collagen fibres
105125.e: Ligaments are made of tightly packed collagen fibres. They are very strong when pulled but only stretch a little.
105125.m: Ligaments are made of strong collagen fibres.

105126.q: How is a torn outer ankle ligament usually treated today?
a: Without surgery, with a splint and physiotherapy
With a plaster cast for a whole year
Not at all, you must keep training straight away
105126.e: Most torn outer ankle ligaments heal well with a supporting splint and targeted exercises. An operation is rarely needed.
105126.m: A torn outer ankle ligament usually heals without surgery.

105127.q: What can happen if a torn ligament heals badly?
a: An unstable joint that keeps giving way
A stiff joint that can never bend again
105127.e: If a ligament stays too long or loose, it no longer holds the joint properly. You then twist it again more easily.
105127.m: A badly healed ligament can make the joint unstable.

105128.q: Roughly how long does a torn ligament take until it can carry weight again?
105128.e: Ligaments have a poor blood supply and heal slowly. It usually takes around six weeks or longer until they hold well again.
105128.m: A torn ligament needs around six weeks to heal.

105129.q: What is the technical term for a dislocated joint?
105129.e: In a luxation, the joint surfaces lose contact with each other. A fracture, on the other hand, is a broken bone.
105129.m: A luxation is a dislocated joint.

105130.q: What is the technical term for putting a dislocated joint back in place?
105130.e: In a reduction, the doctor puts the head of the joint back into its socket, often with painkillers.
105130.m: A reduction puts the joint back in its place.

105131.q: What is it called when a joint is only partly dislocated?
105131.e: In a subluxation, the joint surfaces still partly touch. Often the joint pops back by itself.
105131.m: In a subluxation the joint is only partly dislocated.

105132.q: Which joint easily dislocates in toddlers if they are pulled up sharply by the arm?
a: The head of the radius at the elbow
105132.e: In small children the head of the radius still sits loosely in its holder. A sudden jerk makes it slip partly out, and the child then keeps the arm still.
105132.m: Never pull toddlers up sharply by the arm, or the head of the radius can slip out.

105133.q: In which direction does the kneecap almost always move when it dislocates?
105133.e: The pull of the thigh muscles draws the kneecap slightly outwards. That is why it almost always dislocates to the outer side.
105133.m: When it dislocates, the kneecap usually moves outwards.

105134.q: Why should you not put a dislocated joint back yourself?
a: You could injure nerves, blood vessels or bones
The joint will never go back in
It is forbidden to give first aid
105134.e: Nerves and blood vessels often run next to the joint. There may also be a fracture that only shows up on an X-ray.
105134.m: A dislocated joint needs a doctor.

105135.q: Which parts of a joint are often injured as well in a dislocation?
105135.e: For the bone to jump out of its socket, the capsule and ligaments must be strongly stretched or torn.
105135.m: In a dislocation, the capsule and ligaments often tear too.

105136.q: Why does a shoulder dislocate more easily again after the first time?
a: The capsule and ligaments stay stretched or torn
The upper arm bone gets longer
105136.e: If the injured supporting tissues do not heal tightly together, the joint is less stable. This is common, especially in young people.
105136.m: After a first shoulder dislocation, the joint is often less stable.

105137.q: What happens in a joint with osteoarthritis?
a: The bones become as soft as rubber
105137.e: Osteoarthritis is wear and tear of the joint. The cartilage becomes thinner and cracked until bone can rub on bone.
105137.m: In osteoarthritis, the joint cartilage wears away.

105138.q: What does the ending “-itis” in the word arthritis mean?
105138.e: Arthritis is an inflammation of a joint, osteoarthritis is wear and tear. The two are often confused.

105139.q: In which people does osteoarthritis occur most often?
105139.e: Osteoarthritis is joint wear that develops over many years. That is why it mainly affects older people.

a: A smooth layer on the ends of the bones in a joint
A muscle that moves the joint
A ligament that connects two bones
A fluid in the bone marrow
105140.e: Joint cartilage covers the ends of the bones and makes sure they glide smoothly over each other. In osteoarthritis it wears away.
105140.m: Joint cartilage lets the bones in a joint glide.

105141.q: Which risk factor puts strain on knees and hips and encourages osteoarthritis?
105141.e: Every extra kilogram presses on the joints with every step. That is why being overweight speeds up cartilage wear.
105141.m: Being overweight strains the joints and encourages osteoarthritis.

105142.q: What is a typical early sign of osteoarthritis?
a: Pain in the first steps after a rest
A joint that is always cold
105142.e: This is called start-up pain. After a few minutes of movement it often gets better.
105142.m: Start-up pain after a rest is a typical sign of osteoarthritis.

105143.q: What can often be seen on an X-ray in osteoarthritis?
a: A joint space that has become narrower
105143.e: Cartilage does not show up on an X-ray. When it gets thinner, the bones move closer together and the gap between them looks narrower.
105143.m: A narrow joint space on an X-ray points to osteoarthritis.

105144.q: Which sports are often recommended for osteoarthritis in the knee or hip?
105144.e: These sports move the joints evenly without hard jolts. That keeps muscles and cartilage in good shape.
105144.m: Cycling and swimming are gentle on joints with osteoarthritis.

105145.q: Which two parts of the hip joint does a total hip replacement replace?
a: The hip socket and the head of the thigh bone
The kneecap and the top of the shin bone
The meniscus and the cruciate ligament
105145.e: In a total hip replacement, an artificial socket is placed in the pelvis. A stem with a ball replaces the head of the thigh bone.
105145.m: A total hip replacement replaces the socket and head of the hip joint.

105146.q: What is the most common reason for a hip replacement?
105146.e: When the cartilage is badly damaged, every step hurts. An artificial joint can then take away the pain and improve movement.
105146.m: Most hip replacements are done because of osteoarthritis.

105147.q: Which metal are many implant stems that sit in the thigh bone made of?
105147.e: Titanium is light, very strong and well tolerated by the body. The bone can even grow onto its surface.
105147.m: Many implant stems are made of well-tolerated titanium.

a: A plaster cast for the leg
105148.e: In a hip replacement, surgeons replace the diseased hip joint with an artificial one made of metal, ceramic or plastic.
105148.m: A hip replacement is an artificial hip joint.

105149.q: In which two ways is a hip replacement fixed in the bone?
a: With bone cement or by growing in without cement
With screws from outside through the skin
Only by muscles, with no fixing at all
105149.e: Cemented implants are firm straight away. With cement-free implants, the bone grows into the rough surface.
105149.m: Hip replacements are either cemented or grow into the bone without cement.

105150.q: What does the prefix “endo” in the word endoprosthesis mean?
105150.e: An endoprosthesis is placed inside the body. An artificial leg that is fitted from outside, on the other hand, is an exoprosthesis.
105150.m: An endoprosthesis sits inside the body.

105151.q: In many cases, how long does a modern hip replacement last?
a: Always only until the next winter
105151.e: Thanks to good materials, many hip replacements work for decades. If one becomes loose, it can be replaced.
105151.m: Many hip replacements last twenty years or longer.

105152.q: What material is the artificial head of the hip or the gliding surface of the socket often made of?
105152.e: Ceramic is very hard and smooth, and a special plastic called polyethylene glides well. This means little wear.
105152.m: The hip head and socket are often made of smooth ceramic or plastic.

105153.q: Which complication is especially feared in the first weeks after a hip replacement?
105153.e: Until the muscles and capsule have healed, the artificial head can jump out of the socket. That is why extreme movements are avoided at first.
105153.m: After the operation you must avoid extreme hip movements so the implant does not dislocate.

105154.q: Which animals can also place their thumb opposite their other fingers?
105154.e: Many monkeys and apes also have an opposable thumb. In humans, however, it is especially long and flexible.
105154.m: Many monkeys and apes can also place their thumb opposite their fingers.

105155.q: Which joint can move more, an ellipsoid joint or a ball-and-socket joint?
105155.e: A ball-and-socket joint like the shoulder moves around three axes and can also rotate. An ellipsoid joint has only two axes.
105155.m: A ball-and-socket joint can move more than an ellipsoid joint.

105156.q: What can help with severe osteoarthritis in the knee or hip when nothing else works?
105156.e: If the joint is badly worn, it can be replaced by an implant made of metal and plastic. Afterwards the pain is usually much less.
105156.m: An artificial joint can help with severe osteoarthritis.

105157.q: How can you often tell from the outside that a shoulder is dislocated?
a: The shoulder looks angular with a dent
The shoulder turns completely blue and cold
The shoulder becomes as soft as rubber
105157.e: When the head of the upper arm bone jumps out of the socket, the round shape of the shoulder is missing. A hollow forms below the top of the shoulder.
105157.m: A dislocated shoulder often looks angular and has a dent.

105158.q: What can happen if a torn-off piece of meniscus gets trapped in the knee?
a: Suddenly the knee can no longer be fully straightened
The knee becomes longer for good
The foot goes to sleep for ever
105158.e: The loose piece catches between the bones and blocks the joint. This is called a locked joint.
105158.m: A trapped piece of meniscus can lock the knee.

105159.q: What is a ligament injury called when the ligament is only overstretched but not torn?
105159.e: In a sprain the fibres are overstretched but still whole. It usually heals faster than a tear.
105159.m: A sprained ligament is overstretched but not torn.

105160.q: Which ligament in the knee is injured especially often when skiing?
105160.e: In a fall, the knee often bends inwards while the ski turns outwards. This overstretches or tears the ligament on the inside of the knee.
105160.m: When skiing, the inner ligament of the knee is often injured.

105161.q: Which imaging method shows torn ligaments especially well?
105161.e: An MRI shows soft tissues such as ligaments, cartilage and menisci very precisely. An X-ray, on the other hand, mainly shows bones.
105161.m: Ligaments show up well on an MRI, bones on an X-ray.

105162.q: Apart from heaviness, which property of an object does mass describe?
105162.e: The greater the mass, the harder it is to set an object in motion or slow it down. This property is called inertia.
105162.m: An object with a large mass also has a lot of inertia.

105163.q: How many milligrams are in one gram?
105163.e: The prefix “milli” means one thousandth. So 1 g equals 1000 mg.
105163.m: One gram has a thousand milligrams.

105164.m: To convert kilograms into grams, multiply by a thousand.

105165.q: How does the mass of an ice cube change when it melts completely?
105165.e: When it melts, only the state changes. No water particles are lost, so the mass stays the same.
105165.m: Mass stays the same when something melts.

105166.q: Which symbol is used for mass in physics?
105166.e: The small m stands for mass. g stands for gravitational field strength and F for a force.
105166.m: The symbol for mass is a small m.

105167.q: Three packs of butter each have a mass of 250 g. What is their total mass?
105167.e: Masses can be added: 3 · 250 g = 750 g.
105167.m: You can add the masses of several objects together.

105168.m: Divide grams by a thousand to get kilograms.

105169.q: In which special unit is the mass of gemstones often given?
105169.e: One carat equals 0.2 g. This unit is used for diamonds and other gemstones.
105169.m: The mass of gemstones is measured in carats.

105170.q: In which unit is weight measured?
105170.e: Weight is a force. Forces are measured in newtons, N for short.

105171.q: How do you calculate the weight of an object?
105171.e: Weight equals mass times gravitational field strength, so F = m · g.
105171.m: Weight is the product of mass and gravitational field strength.

105172.q: What is the weight of a child with a mass of 45 kg in Switzerland (field strength 9.81 N/kg)?
105172.e: F = 45 kg · 9.81 N/kg = 441.45 N, so about 441 N.
105172.m: The weight in newtons is about ten times the number of kilograms.

105173.q: Which device measures a weight directly?
105173.e: A newton meter contains a spring that stretches under the load. You read off the force in newtons on the scale.
105173.m: A newton meter shows weight in newtons.

105174.q: How does the weight of an object change if you double its mass in the same place?
105174.e: Weight is mass times field strength. If the place stays the same, it grows in the same proportion as the mass.
105174.m: Twice the mass means twice the weight in the same place.

105175.q: An object has a weight of 30 N on Earth. What is its mass if you use 10 N/kg?
105175.e: m = F ÷ g = 30 N ÷ 10 N/kg = 3 kg.
105175.m: You get the mass by dividing the weight by the field strength.

105176.q: What do bathroom scales actually measure?
a: The weight, which they convert into kilograms
The mass directly, regardless of location
105176.e: The scales measure how hard you press on them. They convert this value into kilograms using the Earth's field strength.

105177.q: Why do astronauts float in the ISS space station?
a: They are constantly falling round the Earth together with the station
There is no gravity at all in space
The station pushes them up with air
105177.e: Even at a height of 400 km the Earth still pulls strongly. But the station and the people fall round the Earth together, so they feel no weight.
105177.m: In the space station you float because everything falls round the Earth together.

105178.q: Two children of 35 kg and 40 kg sit on a bench. What weight do they exert on the bench together (10 N/kg)?
105178.e: Together they have 75 kg. F = 75 kg · 10 N/kg = 750 N.
105178.m: The weights of several objects can be added together.

105179.q: Roughly what is the gravitational field strength in Switzerland?
105179.e: In central Europe the field strength is about 9.81 N/kg. In lessons people often simplify it to 10 N/kg.
105179.m: In Switzerland the field strength is about 9.81 N/kg.

105180.q: Where is the gravitational field strength much greater than on Earth?
a: At the surface of the Sun
On the summit of Mount Everest
105180.e: The Sun has an enormous mass. At its surface, almost thirty times more force acts on each kilogram than on Earth. On the Moon and Mars the field strength is smaller.
105180.m: At the Sun's surface the field strength is almost thirty times that on Earth.

105181.q: Why is the gravitational field strength smaller at the equator than at the poles?
a: The Earth is wider there and spins faster
It is warmer at the equator
There is more water at the equator
The air is thinner at the equator
105181.e: The Earth bulges slightly at the equator, so you stand further from the centre. Also, the Earth's rotation pushes outwards most strongly there.
105181.m: The Earth's flattening and rotation make the field strength smaller at the equator.

105182.q: Which unit is the unit N/kg equal to?
105182.e: One newton is 1 kg · m/s². Dividing by kg leaves m/s². That is why the field strength equals the acceleration due to gravity.
105182.m: Field strength in N/kg is the same as the acceleration due to gravity in m/s².

105183.q: On which planet in our solar system is the gravitational field strength at the surface greatest?
105183.e: Jupiter is the most massive planet. Its field strength at the cloud tops is about 25 N/kg.
105183.m: Jupiter has the greatest field strength of all the planets.

105184.q: How does the gravitational field strength on the summit of the Matterhorn compare with Zurich?
105184.e: On the summit you are further from the Earth's centre. Attraction decreases with distance, even if only a little.
105184.m: The higher you climb, the very slightly smaller the field strength.

105185.q: What does the gravitational field strength tell you?
a: The weight per kilogram of mass
The speed of a falling stone
105185.e: The field strength tells you how many newtons act on each kilogram. On Earth it is about 9.81 N per kg.
105185.m: The field strength gives the weight per kilogram.

105186.q: Which planet has a gravitational field strength very similar to Earth's?
105186.e: Venus is almost as big and heavy as the Earth. Its field strength is about 8.9 N/kg.
105186.m: On Venus gravity is almost as strong as on Earth.

105187.q: A lunar vehicle has a mass of 120 kg. What is its weight on the Moon (field strength 1.6 N/kg)?
105187.m: On the Moon you calculate weight with a field strength of 1.6 N/kg.

105188.q: An object has a weight of 80 N on the Moon. What is its mass (field strength 1.6 N/kg)?
105188.m: Mass is weight divided by field strength.

105189.q: A rucksack has a mass of 6 kg. What is its weight on the Moon (field strength 1.6 N/kg)?
105189.e: F = 6 kg · 1.6 N/kg = 9.6 N. On Earth it would be about 60 N.
105189.m: On the Moon weight is much smaller than on Earth.

105190.q: A spring balance shows 6 N on Earth. Roughly what does it show on the Moon?
105190.e: The spring balance measures weight. On the Moon it is only about a sixth: 6 N ÷ 6 = 1 N.
105190.m: On the Moon a newton meter shows only about a sixth.

105191.q: Why is it still hard to push a big boulder sideways on the Moon?
a: Its mass is the same as on Earth
There is no friction on the Moon
It is too cold on the Moon
105191.e: Weight is smaller on the Moon, but mass is not. To set an object moving, what matters is its mass.
105191.m: Even on the Moon a rock with a large mass is hard to push.

105192.q: Roughly what fraction of the Earth's mass does the Moon have?
105192.e: The Earth has about 81 times as much mass as the Moon. But because the Moon is also much smaller, its gravity at the surface is not 81 times weaker, only a few times weaker than on Earth.
105192.m: The Moon has only just over one per cent of the Earth's mass.

105193.q: A rock sample has a weight of 3.2 N on the Moon. What is its weight on Earth (Moon 1.6 N/kg, Earth 10 N/kg)?
105193.e: First the mass: 3.2 N ÷ 1.6 N/kg = 2 kg. On Earth: 2 kg · 10 N/kg = 20 N.
105193.m: Using the mass, you can convert weights from one world to another.

105194.q: An astronaut jumps on Mars with the same push-off as on Earth. Roughly how high does she get in comparison?
a: About two and a half times as high
105194.e: On Mars gravity pulls with only about 38 per cent of Earth's gravity. With the same push-off you get about 9.81 ÷ 3.7, so roughly 2.6 times as high.
105194.m: With weaker gravity you jump higher.

105195.q: How strong is gravity on Mars compared with Earth?
a: A little more than a third
105195.e: On Mars only about 38 per cent of the force that acts on Earth acts on each mass.
105195.m: On Mars you weigh a little more than a third of your Earth weight.

105196.q: What is the weight of a 50 kg person on Mars (field strength 3.7 N/kg)?
105196.m: Weight on Mars is calculated with 3.7 N/kg.

105197.q: A Mars rover has a mass of 1000 kg. What is its weight on Mars (field strength 3.7 N/kg)?
105197.m: A rover presses down on the ground much less on Mars than on Earth.

105198.q: How big is the diameter of Mars compared with the Earth?
105198.e: Mars has a diameter of about 6800 km, the Earth about 12,700 km. So Mars is about half as wide as the Earth.
105198.m: Mars is about half as wide as the Earth.

105199.q: Bathroom scales show 30 kg on Earth. Roughly what would they show on Mars?
105199.e: The scales measure weight. On Mars it is about 38 per cent: 30 kg · 0.38 gives about 11 kg.
105199.m: On Mars bathroom scales show just over a third.

105200.q: Roughly what fraction of the Earth's mass does Mars have?
105200.e: Mars has only about 11 per cent of the Earth's mass. That is why it attracts objects at its surface more weakly.
105200.m: Mars has only about a tenth of the Earth's mass.

105201.q: Roughly how many times stronger is gravity on Mars than on the Moon?
105201.e: 3.7 N/kg divided by 1.6 N/kg gives about 2.3.
105201.m: Gravity on Mars is just over twice as strong as on the Moon.

105202.q: How do you calculate the density of an object?
105202.e: Density ρ (rho) is m ÷ V. It tells you how much mass there is in each unit of volume.
105202.m: Density is mass divided by volume.

105203.q: In which unit is the density of solids often given?
105203.e: Mass in grams divided by volume in cubic centimetres gives the unit grams per cubic centimetre.
105203.m: The density of solids is often given in g/cm³.

105204.q: A stone has a mass of 60 g and a volume of 20 cm³. What is its density?
105204.m: For density, divide the mass by the volume.

105205.q: How many kg/m³ are equal to 1 g/cm³?
105205.e: A cubic metre has 1,000,000 cm³. 1,000,000 g is 1000 kg. So 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.
105205.m: One gram per cubic centimetre is a thousand kilograms per cubic metre.

105206.q: Why does cooking oil float on water?
a: Oil has a lower density than water
Oil has a higher density than water
105206.e: A substance with a lower density rises in a substance with a higher density. Cooking oil has about 0.9 g/cm³.
105206.m: Oil floats on top because it is less dense than water.

105207.q: Roughly what is the mass of one cubic metre of air at sea level?
105207.e: The density of air at sea level and 20 °C is about 1.2 kg/m³. So air is light, but not without mass.
105207.m: One cubic metre of air has a mass of just over one kilogram.

105208.q: Which of these substances has the greatest density?
105208.e: Glass has a density of about 2.5 g/cm³ and sinks in water. Cork and polystyrene are much less dense than water.
105208.m: Glass is denser than water, so it sinks.

105209.q: One litre of a liquid has a mass of 750 g. What is its density?
105209.e: 1 litre is 1000 cm³. ρ = 750 g ÷ 1000 cm³ = 0.75 g/cm³.
105209.m: For density, first convert litres into cubic centimetres.

105210.q: How many cubic centimetres are in one litre?
105210.e: One litre is one cubic decimetre. 1 dm³ = 10 cm · 10 cm · 10 cm = 1000 cm³.
105210.m: One litre has a thousand cubic centimetres.

105211.q: What volume is one millilitre equal to?
105211.e: A millilitre is one thousandth of a litre. It exactly fills a cube with 1 cm edges.
105211.m: A millilitre is the same as a cubic centimetre.

105212.q: How do you read the water level in a measuring cylinder correctly?
a: At eye level, at the lowest point of the curved surface
From above at an angle, at the highest edge
At the edge where the water creeps up
105212.e: Water forms a downward-curving surface. You read it at the lowest point and look at it horizontally.
105212.m: With a measuring cylinder, read at eye level at the lowest point.

105213.q: What is the volume of a cube with 3 cm edges?
105213.m: The volume of a cube is edge times edge times edge.

105214.q: What is the base unit of volume in the International System of Units?
105214.e: In the SI system, the cubic metre is the unit of volume. The litre is an accepted additional unit.
105214.m: The SI unit of volume is the cubic metre.

105215.q: What is a displacement can (overflow can) used for in physics lessons?
a: To find the volume of irregular objects
To measure the temperature of water
105215.e: You cannot simply measure a stone with a ruler. In the displacement can it pushes out water, and this water equals its volume.
105215.m: A displacement can measures the volume of oddly shaped objects.

105216.q: How full must the displacement can be before measuring?
a: So full that water has only just stopped running out
Just below the spout, with plenty of air
105216.e: Only if the can is filled up to the spout does exactly the displaced water flow out when the object is put in.
105216.m: The displacement can must first be filled up to the spout.

105217.q: What do you catch the overflowing water in when using a displacement can?
105217.e: The displaced water runs into a measuring cylinder. You can read off its volume there directly.
105217.m: The displaced water is caught in a measuring cylinder.

105218.q: A stone is put into the full displacement can, and 35 ml of water flow out. What is the stone's volume?
105218.e: The stone displaces exactly as much water as the space it takes up. 35 ml equals 35 cm³.
105218.m: The displaced water has the same volume as the submerged object.

105219.q: A stone with a volume of 35 cm³ has a mass of 91 g. What is its density?
105219.m: With scales and a displacement can you can find the density of a stone.

105220.q: What must you do to measure the volume of a cork in a displacement can?
a: Push it completely under water, for example with a needle
105220.e: Cork floats and only sinks in partly by itself. Only when it is fully under water does it displace its whole volume.
105220.m: Floating objects must be fully submerged to measure their volume.

105221.q: A measuring cylinder holds 50 ml of water. After a key is dropped in, it shows 72 ml. What is the volume of the key?
105221.e: You work out the difference: 72 ml minus 50 ml = 22 ml, so 22 cm³. This also works without a displacement can.
105221.m: The difference between the water levels gives the object's volume.

105222.q: What can spoil a measurement with a displacement can?
a: Air bubbles stuck to the object
105222.e: Air bubbles push out extra water. The measured volume is then too big.
105222.m: Air bubbles on the object make the volume measurement inaccurate.

105223.q: What is Archimedes said to have shouted when the solution came to him in the bath?
105223.e: Eureka is Greek and means “I have found it”. In the bath Archimedes noticed that his body pushed water aside.
105223.m: Archimedes shouted “Eureka”, I have found it.

105224.q: On which island was Syracuse, the home town of Archimedes?
105224.e: Syracuse lies on the east coast of Sicily. In Archimedes' time it was a rich Greek city.
105224.m: Archimedes lived in Syracuse on Sicily.

105225.q: What trick did the king fear the goldsmith had played?
a: That he had mixed silver into the gold
That he had carved the crown from wood
That he had not made the crown at all
That he had used too many gemstones
105225.e: The king suspected the goldsmith had kept some of the gold and replaced it with cheaper silver.
105225.m: The king feared his crown contained silver instead of pure gold.

105226.q: Why does a crown containing silver displace more water than a lump of gold of the same mass?
a: Silver has a lower density and takes up more space
Silver has a higher density than gold
105226.e: For the same mass, a substance with a lower density takes up more volume. That is why the mixed crown displaces more water.
105226.m: For the same mass, a less dense substance needs more space.

105227.q: A crown made of pure gold has a mass of 965 g. What is its volume (density of gold 19.3 g/cm³)?
105227.e: V = m ÷ ρ = 965 g ÷ 19.3 g/cm³ = 50 cm³.
105227.m: You get the volume by dividing the mass by the density.

105228.q: A crown containing silver and a lump of gold of the same mass hang on a beam balance. What happens when both are fully dipped in water?
a: The side with the crown goes up
The side with the gold goes up
The crown sinks to the bottom
105228.e: Because of the silver, the crown has more volume and displaces more water. It therefore gets more upthrust and seems lighter.
105228.m: More volume means more upthrust under water.

105229.q: An object displaces 2 litres of water when submerged. Roughly how big is the upthrust (10 N/kg)?
105229.e: 2 litres of water have a mass of 2 kg. Their weight is 2 kg · 10 N/kg = 20 N.
105229.m: Every litre of water displaced gives about 10 N of upthrust.

105230.q: What is the International Prototype Kilogram?
a: A metal cylinder that defined exactly one kilogram for a long time
A tank holding exactly one litre of water
105230.e: The International Prototype Kilogram is a small metal cylinder near Paris. From 1889 to 2019 its mass was exactly one kilogram.
105230.m: The prototype kilogram was the standard for the kilogram for a long time.

105231.q: Why do we need a precisely defined standard for the kilogram?
a: So that things are weighed the same everywhere in the world
So that nothing needs weighing any more
105231.e: Only with a shared standard does a kilogram mean the same in Switzerland as in Japan or Brazil. This matters for trade and science.
105231.m: A fixed standard makes sure things are weighed the same everywhere.

105232.q: Why was the prototype kilogram kept under glass bell jars?
a: So that dust and dirt would not change its mass
So that it would not roll away
So that it would glow in the dark
So that it would always stay cold
105232.e: Even a tiny speck of dust would change the mass. The bell jars protected the cylinder from dust and dirt.
105232.m: Glass bell jars protected the prototype kilogram from dust.

105233.q: How was the kilogram originally defined, before the prototype kilogram?
a: As the mass of a litre of water
As the mass of one of the king's gold bars
As the mass of 1000 grains of wheat
As the mass of a paving stone
105233.e: In France at the end of the 18th century, the kilogram was defined as the mass of a cubic decimetre of water.
105233.m: Originally a kilogram was the mass of a litre of water.

105234.q: Why is the kilogram no longer defined by the prototype kilogram today?
a: Because a metal cylinder can change slightly over time
Because it was too heavy to carry
105234.e: Comparisons showed that the mass of the prototype and its copies differed by tiny amounts. Since 2019 the kilogram has therefore been based on a constant of nature.
105234.m: Since 2019 the kilogram has been tied to a constant of nature.

105235.q: What is a constant of nature, like the one that defines the kilogram today?
a: A quantity that is the same everywhere in the universe
A number that is worked out anew each year
A set of scales in a laboratory
105235.e: Constants of nature do not change and are the same everywhere. That makes them better than a metal cylinder for defining units.
105235.m: Constants of nature are the same everywhere and always.

105236.q: A parcel has a mass of 2.5 kg. How many grams is that?
105236.e: One kilogram is 1000 grams. 2.5 · 1000 g = 2500 g.
105236.m: One kilogram has a thousand grams.

105237.q: To how many grams can an analytical balance in a laboratory often weigh accurately?
105237.e: Analytical balances often show four decimal places. 0.0001 g is 0.1 milligrams.
105237.m: An analytical balance weighs to a tenth of a milligram.

105238.q: Why does a precision balance often have a glass case around the weighing pan?
a: So that draughts do not disturb the measurement
So that nobody can see the result
So that it does not rust
105238.e: Even a slight draught presses on the weighing pan. The draught shield stops the display from wobbling.
105238.m: The glass case protects the precision balance from draughts.

105239.q: How can you tell that a precision balance is standing level?
a: The air bubble in the spirit level is in the middle
105239.e: The bubble level is a small spirit level. Only when the balance is level does it measure accurately.
105239.m: A precision balance must be levelled using its bubble level.

105240.q: Why should you not put warm objects on a precision balance?
a: Rising warm air distorts the reading
The balance then shows the temperature
105240.e: Air rises above a warm object and pulls slightly upwards. The reading is then too low and unsteady.
105240.m: Only weigh objects at room temperature on a precision balance.

105241.q: How do you check whether a precision balance measures correctly?
a: With a test weight of known mass
With a glass of an unknown amount of water
105241.e: You put on a weight whose mass is known exactly. If the display differs, the balance is adjusted.
105241.m: A test weight checks the accuracy of a balance.

105242.q: Where is the best place to set up a precision balance?
105242.e: Vibrations, draughts and heat disturb the delicate measurement. Special weighing tables are heavy and stand steady.
105242.m: A precision balance needs a calm, solid place.

105243.q: Why must an electronic precision balance be readjusted after moving from Bern to Zermatt?
a: The gravitational field strength is slightly different in each place
Zermatt uses a different unit of mass
The balance loses weight during transport
105243.e: Electronic balances measure a force and convert it into mass. Because the field strength varies slightly with place and altitude, they need to be reset.
105243.m: An electronic balance must be readjusted in a new place.

105244.q: Where are precision balances needed particularly often?
105244.e: In laboratories and pharmacies, tiny amounts of substances have to be weighed exactly, for example for medicines.
105244.m: In laboratories and pharmacies, tiny amounts are weighed on precision balances.

105245.q: Silver has a density of about 10.5 g/cm³. What does that mean?
a: A 1 cm³ cube of silver has a mass of 10.5 g
10.5 cm³ of silver have a mass of 1 g
105245.e: Density tells you the mass of one cubic centimetre of a substance. For silver it is about 10.5 g, roughly ten times more than water.
105245.m: Density tells you how much a cubic centimetre of a substance weighs.

105246.q: Why is a lot of aluminium used in building aircraft?
a: It has a low density of about 2.7 g/cm³
It is liquid at room temperature
105246.e: Aluminium is about three times less dense than steel. This keeps the aircraft light so it uses less fuel.
105246.m: Aluminium is light because it has a low density.

105247.q: Which of these metals has the greatest density?
105247.e: Gold has a density of about 19.3 g/cm³. Iron has about 7.9, copper about 9 and aluminium only 2.7 g/cm³.
105247.m: Gold is a very dense metal.

105248.q: Which metal is so light that it floats on water?
105248.e: Lithium has a density of only about 0.53 g/cm³. However, it reacts violently with water.
105248.m: Lithium is the lightest metal and floats on water.

105249.q: Why does an iron nail sink in water?
a: Iron has a greater density than water
105249.e: Iron is about eight times denser than water. An object that is denser than the liquid sinks in it.

105250.q: Why does an iron cube float on liquid mercury?
a: Mercury has a greater density than iron
105250.e: Mercury has a density of about 13.5 g/cm³, so it is denser than iron. The less dense object floats on top.
105250.m: A metal floats on a liquid that is denser than itself.

105251.q: Why are lead weights used to weigh down fishing lines?
a: Lead has a high density and is cheap
105251.e: Lead has a density of about 11.3 g/cm³. So even a small piece is quite heavy. Because it is poisonous, it is often replaced today.
105251.m: Lead is dense, which makes it good as a weight.

105252.q: A copper cube has a volume of 10 cm³. What is its mass (density 8.96 g/cm³)?

105253.q: A piece of aluminium has a mass of 54 g. What is its volume (density 2.7 g/cm³)?
105253.e: V = m ÷ ρ = 54 g ÷ 2.7 g/cm³ = 20 cm³.
105253.m: Volume is mass divided by density.

105254.q: Why is even a small gold bar surprisingly heavy?
a: Gold has a very high density
105254.e: Gold has a density of about 19.3 g/cm³. A cube with 10 cm edges would already have a mass of over 19 kg.
105254.m: Gold is very heavy because of its high density.

105255.q: What are the usually green, outermost leaves of a flower called?
105255.e: The sepals form the outermost ring of the flower’s covering. They are usually green and inconspicuous.
105255.m: The sepals form the outermost ring of a flower.

105256.q: What is the main job of the sepals while the flower is still a bud?
105256.e: The sepals wrap around the young flower bud and protect the delicate inner parts from cold, drying out and being eaten.
105256.m: The sepals protect the flower while it is a bud.

105257.q: What do you call all the sepals of a flower together?
105257.e: All the sepals together form the calyx. It can consist of separate sepals or of sepals that have grown together.
105257.m: All the sepals of a flower together form the calyx.

105258.q: In the dandelion the calyx has turned into a ring of hairs. What is it for?
105258.e: The ring of hairs (pappus) is a modified calyx. It works like a parachute, so the wind can carry the fruits far away.
105258.m: The parachute of the dandelion fruit is a modified calyx.

105259.q: In which garden plant are the sepals not green but bright red or pink?
105259.e: In the fuchsia the four spreading sepals are strikingly coloured. In this way they help to attract pollinators.
105259.m: In the fuchsia the sepals are coloured too.

105260.q: Which green flower part sits at the top of a picked strawberry?
105260.e: In the strawberry the calyx remains after flowering. It sits as a green ring at the top of the fruit.
105260.m: The green ring on a strawberry is the calyx of the former flower.

105261.q: In the Christmas rose, the large white leaves of the flower look like petals. What are they really?
105261.e: In the Christmas rose the large, white sepals take over the job of the petals. The real petals have turned into small nectar containers.
105261.m: In the Christmas rose the white showy leaves are sepals.

105262.q: What do you call an extra outer ring of sepal-like leaves, like the one in the strawberry or mallow?
105262.e: Some flowers have a second ring of small leaves below the real calyx. This is called the epicalyx.
105262.m: Some flowers have an epicalyx below the calyx.

105263.q: What do you call all the petals of a flower together?
105263.e: All the petals of a flower together form the corolla. It lies inside the calyx.
105263.m: All the petals together form the corolla.

105264.q: Why are the petals of many flowers brightly coloured?
105264.e: Coloured petals work like an advertising sign. Insects find the flower more easily and pollinate it when they visit.

105265.q: In which kind of light do bees see patterns on many petals that are invisible to people?
105265.e: Bees can see ultraviolet light. Many flowers have patterns that can only be seen in UV light.
105265.m: Bees see flower patterns in ultraviolet light.

105266.q: How many petals does a flower of the cabbage family have, for example oilseed rape?
105266.e: Plants of the cabbage family have four petals arranged in a cross. That is why the family is also called the crucifers, from the Latin for cross.
105266.m: The cabbage family has four petals in the shape of a cross.

105267.q: In which flower have the petals grown together into a bell or tube?
105267.e: In the gentian the joined petals form a bell. In the rose and oilseed rape the petals are separate.
105267.m: In the gentian the petals have grown together into a bell.

105268.q: What are the coloured spots or lines on petals called that show insects the way to the nectar?
105268.e: Nectar guides are markings on the petals. Like signposts, they lead insects to the nectar.
105268.m: Nectar guides show insects the way to the nectar.

105269.q: Which plant family has flowers with a ‘standard’, ‘wings’ and a ‘keel’?
105269.e: In the pea family, such as clover, pea or bean, the petals are shaped into a standard, two wings and a keel.
105269.m: Pea flowers consist of a standard, wings and a keel.

105270.q: What happens to the petals of most flowers after pollination?
105270.e: After pollination the flower no longer needs to attract anything. The petals wilt and fall off while the fruit develops.

105271.q: Which leaves of a flower lie just outside the petals and protect the bud?
105271.e: The usually green sepals wrap around the young bud. When the flower opens, they sit on the outside below the petals.

105272.q: In which part of the stamen is pollen made?
105272.e: The anther at the tip of the stamen contains pollen sacs. That is where the pollen grains form.
105272.m: Pollen is made in the anther.

105273.q: What is the thin stalk that holds up the anther called?
105273.e: A stamen consists of the filament and the anther. The filament holds the anther in the right position.
105273.m: The filament holds up the anther.

105275.q: What do you call a flower that has only stamens but no carpels?
105275.e: Stamens make the pollen and count as the male organs of the flower. So a flower with only stamens is called a male flower.
105275.m: A flower with only stamens is a male flower.

105276.q: What is a flower called that has both stamens and carpels?
105276.e: Most flowering plants have hermaphrodite flowers. In them, stamens and carpels are in the same flower.
105276.m: A hermaphrodite flower has stamens and carpels.

105277.q: The hazel has flowers with stamens and flowers with carpels on the same bush. What are such plants called?
105277.e: When separate male and female flowers grow on the same plant, the plant is called monoecious.
105277.m: In monoecious plants both kinds of flower grow on the same plant.

105278.q: What do you call flowers in which many stamens have turned into extra petals, as in many garden roses?
105278.e: In double flowers, breeding has turned stamens into petals. Such flowers often offer insects hardly any pollen.
105278.m: Double flowers have extra petals instead of many stamens.

105279.q: Why is the white dead-nettle called ‘dead’?
a: It does not sting like the stinging nettle
It only grows in the dark
105279.e: The dead-nettle looks like the stinging nettle but has no stinging hairs. ‘Dead’ here means that it does not have the stinging effect. It belongs to the mint family.
105279.m: The dead-nettle looks like a stinging nettle but does not sting.

105280.q: What is the lowest, thickened part of the pistil called?
105280.e: At the bottom the pistil is thickened into the ovary. The ovules lie inside it.
105280.m: The ovary is the thickened base of the pistil.

105281.q: What do you call a fruit like the strawberry, where the receptacle helps to form it as well as the ovary?
105281.e: In the strawberry the receptacle becomes the red flesh. Because more than just the ovary is involved, it is called a false fruit.
105281.m: The strawberry is a false fruit.

105282.q: What develops from the ovules in the ovary?
105282.e: The egg cells lie in the ovules. After fertilisation the ovules develop into seeds.

105283.q: Where do you find the ovary in a tulip flower?
a: In the middle of the flower
At the tip of the petals
105283.e: The ovary is the thick, lower part of the pistil. In the tulip you can see it well in the middle of the flower, surrounded by the stamens.
105283.m: The ovary sits in the middle of the flower.

105284.q: In which fruit can you still see the dried remains of the flower at the bottom, because the ovary sat below them?
105284.e: In the apple the ovary lies below where the flower’s covering is attached. That is why the remains of the calyx stay at the bottom of the fruit.
105284.m: On an apple you can still see the remains of the calyx at the bottom.

105285.q: Which three parts together form the pistil of a flower?
105285.e: The pistil consists of the ovary at the bottom, the style above it and the stigma at the very top.
105285.m: The pistil consists of ovary, style and stigma.

105286.q: From which part of the ovary does the juicy flesh of a cherry develop?
105286.e: The wall of the ovary becomes the fruit wall. In the cherry it forms the skin, the flesh and the hard stone.
105286.m: The flesh of the cherry develops from the wall of the ovary.

105287.q: What is the fruit of the pea called, in which the seeds lie in a row?
105287.e: The pea pod develops from the ovary. Inside it the peas, which are really the seeds, lie in a row.

105288.q: What is the very top of the pistil called, which catches the pollen?
105288.e: The stigma sits at the very top of the pistil. If suitable pollen lands there, the flower has been pollinated.

105289.q: Why is the stigma of many flowers sticky?
a: So that pollen sticks to it
105289.e: A sticky surface holds the pollen grains in place. So the pollen stays on the stigma until it germinates.
105289.m: A sticky stigma holds the pollen in place.

105290.q: What do the stigmas of wind-pollinated grasses usually look like?
105290.e: Feathery stigmas have a large surface. With it they catch pollen grains from the air like a net.
105290.m: Grasses catch pollen from the air with feathery stigmas.

105291.q: In Mund in the canton of Valais, a spice made from dried flower stigmas is harvested. Which one?
105291.e: Saffron consists of the stigmas of the saffron crocus. It has been grown in Mund in Upper Valais for centuries.
105291.m: Saffron consists of dried crocus stigmas.

105292.q: Why is saffron one of the most expensive spices in the world?
a: The tiny stigmas are picked by hand
It only grows on the Moon
It has to ripen for a hundred years
105292.e: Each saffron flower gives only three fine stigma threads. They are picked by hand, and you need a great many flowers for one gram of saffron.
105292.m: Saffron is expensive because the stigmas are harvested by hand.

105293.q: What grows out of a pollen grain after it has landed on a suitable stigma?
105293.e: The pollen grain germinates on the stigma. It forms a fine pollen tube that grows down inside.
105293.m: On the stigma the pollen germinates into a pollen tube.

105294.q: What is it called when pollen reaches the stigma of a flower?
105294.e: In pollination, pollen reaches the stigma, often with the help of insects or the wind. Only after that can a fruit form.
105294.m: Pollination means pollen lands on the stigma.

105295.q: What are the long ‘hairs’ hanging out of the top of a young corn cob?
105295.e: Each kernel of maize had a very long style with a stigma. These threads stick out of the cob and catch pollen.
105295.m: The threads on a corn cob are long styles with stigmas.

105296.q: Which part of the pistil connects the stigma to the ovary?
105296.e: The style is the stalk-like middle part of the pistil. It holds the stigma up and connects it to the ovary.
105296.m: The style connects the stigma and the ovary.

105297.q: Through which part does the pollen tube grow down to the ovary?
105297.e: The pollen tube grows from the stigma through the tissue of the style. In this way it reaches the ovules in the ovary.
105297.m: The pollen tube grows through the style.

105298.q: What does the pollen tube bring to the ovule?
a: The sperm cells of the pollen
105298.e: The sperm cells travel down the pollen tube to the egg cell in the ovule. Fertilisation takes place there.
105298.m: The pollen tube brings the sperm cells to the egg cell.

105299.q: The cowslip has flowers with a long style and flowers with a short style. What does this encourage?
105299.e: Insects carry pollen from one flower form to the other. Pollen from the same form hardly works, so different plants are crossed.
105299.m: Styles of different lengths help the cowslip cross with other plants.

105300.q: In traveller’s joy, what forms the long, feathery tails on the fruits after flowering?
105300.e: In traveller’s joy the styles grow into feathery tails after flowering. With these the wind carries the fruits away.
105300.m: In traveller’s joy the styles become the flight feathers of the fruits.

105301.q: Which three parts make up the pistil of a flower?
105301.e: At the top of the pistil sits the sticky stigma, below it the style and at the bottom the ovary. The pistil is the female organ of the flower.
105301.m: The pistil consists of stigma, style and ovary.

105302.q: How many styles does an apple blossom have?
105302.e: The apple blossom has five styles. They belong to five carpels, which later form the core.
105302.m: An apple blossom has five styles.

105303.q: How did the cranesbill get its name?
105303.e: After flowering, the column of styles grows into a long beak. So the fruit looks like the beak of a crane.
105303.m: The cranesbill has a fruit shaped like a beak.

105304.q: Which of these plants is pollinated by the wind?
105304.e: Rye is a grass. Like many grasses, it lets the wind spread its pollen.
105304.m: Cereals such as rye are pollinated by the wind.

105305.q: Why are the flowers of wind-pollinated plants usually inconspicuous?
a: They do not need to attract animals
They only grow in the shade
105305.e: The wind does not react to colours or scents. That is why wind-pollinated plants save on colourful petals, scent and nectar.
105305.m: Wind-pollinated flowers do not need colourful petals.

105306.q: Why do wind-pollinated plants make especially large amounts of pollen?
a: Because most of it is lost
105306.e: The wind spreads pollen at random. Only a tiny part lands on a suitable stigma, so huge amounts are needed.
105306.m: Wind-pollinated plants make huge amounts of pollen.

105307.q: Which wind-pollinated tree is one of the most common causes of pollen allergies in Switzerland in spring?
105307.e: The birch releases large amounts of pollen into the air in March and April. Birch pollen is one of the most important allergens in Switzerland in spring.
105307.m: Birch pollen causes many allergies in spring.

105308.q: What is the pollen of wind-pollinated plants usually like?
105308.e: Light, dry pollen floats well in the air. Sticky pollen, on the other hand, is typical of flowers pollinated by insects.
105308.m: Wind pollen is light and dry.

105309.q: In which crop do the male tassels sit at the top and the female cobs further down, so that the wind spreads the pollen?
105309.e: In maize the male flower clusters stand as a tassel at the tip. The pollen trickles down with the wind onto the cobs of the same plant and neighbouring plants.
105309.m: In maize the wind carries pollen from the tassel to the cob.

105310.q: Which federal office measures pollen in the air in Switzerland and publishes pollen forecasts?
105310.e: MeteoSwiss runs a national pollen monitoring network. It gives daily information about how much pollen is in the air.
105310.m: MeteoSwiss measures pollen in the air in Switzerland.

105311.q: Which trees sometimes colour puddles and cars with yellow pollen in spring?
105311.e: Spruces and pines are conifers and are pollinated by the wind. Their pollen flies in such large amounts that it forms yellow layers.
105311.m: Conifers spread huge amounts of yellow pollen in spring.

105312.q: Why do hazels and alders flower before their leaves come out?
a: Leaves would slow down the pollen
Leaves need the pollen as fertiliser
105312.e: Without leaves, the wind can carry the pollen through the branches unhindered. So it reaches the stigmas of other plants more easily.
105312.m: Many wind-pollinated trees flower before their leaves come out.

105313.q: Which sugary liquid do many flowers offer insects as a reward?
105313.e: Nectar is a sweet juice from special glands in the flower. Insects drink it and pick up pollen at the same time.
105313.m: Nectar is the sweet reward for flower visitors.

105314.q: Which insect carries pollen home in ‘baskets’ on its back legs?
105314.e: Honeybees have a hollow with hairs on their back legs, the pollen basket. In it they press the pollen into little balls.
105314.m: Honeybees carry pollen in baskets on their back legs.

105315.q: Roughly how many species of wild bee live in Switzerland?
105315.e: About 600 species of wild bee are known in Switzerland, for example mason bees and bumblebees. They are important pollinators.
105315.m: Hundreds of species of wild bee live in Switzerland.

105316.q: Which insects mainly pollinate the strongly scented flowers of honeysuckle at night?
105316.e: Honeysuckle smells especially strong in the evening. With their long tongues, moths can reach the nectar in the long flower tube.
105316.m: Moths pollinate flowers with long tubes at night.

105317.q: What do you call flowers that attract flies with a smell of rotting meat?
105317.e: Carrion flowers copy the smell of dead animals. Flies and beetles looking for carrion visit the flower and carry pollen as they do so.
105317.m: Carrion flowers attract flies with the smell of rotting meat.

105318.q: Why is red clover mainly pollinated by bumblebees?
105318.e: In red clover the nectar lies deep in narrow flower tubes. Long-tongued bumblebees can reach it better than many other insects.
105318.m: With their long tongues, bumblebees reach the nectar in red clover.

105319.q: What do bees collect pollen for?
a: As building material for the honeycomb
As fuel for heating in winter
105319.e: Pollen contains a lot of protein. Bees feed their larvae with it; the wax for the honeycomb, on the other hand, they make themselves.
105319.m: Pollen is the protein food for young bees.

105320.q: How do honeybees show other bees in the hive where a rich source of flowers is?
105320.e: With the waggle dance, forager bees pass on the direction and distance of a food source. Karl von Frisch studied this dance language.
105320.m: Honeybees use the waggle dance to show the way to flowers.

a: Pollen reaches the stigma of the same plant
105321.e: In self-pollination the pollen comes from the same flower or from the same plant. No partner is needed.
105321.m: In self-pollination the pollen comes from the same plant.

105322.q: Which of these crops usually pollinates itself?
105322.e: In the pea the flower is usually pollinated before it even opens. Rye, sweet cherry and apple, on the other hand, usually need pollen from another plant.

105323.q: What is the disadvantage of self-pollination over many generations?
105323.e: If plants always pollinate themselves, no new genes are mixed in. The offspring become more and more alike.

105324.q: What is the advantage of self-pollination for a plant?
105324.e: With self-pollination the plant does not depend on insects, wind or neighbouring plants. It can reproduce on its own.

105325.q: In summer, violets form flowers that never open. How are they still pollinated?
a: They pollinate themselves inside the closed bud
105325.e: Such closed flowers are called cleistogamous. Pollen and stigma lie so close together in the bud that the flower reliably pollinates itself.

105326.q: Which scientist used self-pollinating peas to discover the laws of inheritance?
105326.e: In the 19th century Gregor Mendel crossed peas in his monastery garden. Because peas normally pollinate themselves, he could cross pure lines in a controlled way.
105326.m: Gregor Mendel discovered the rules of inheritance with peas.

105327.q: What do you call plants whose own pollen on the stigma does not lead to fertilisation?
105327.e: Self-sterile plants recognise and block their own pollen. They need pollen from another plant of their species.

105328.q: Tomato flowers pollinate themselves when the pollen is shaken out. Which insects are used for this in greenhouses?
105328.e: When bumblebees visit a flower they make their flight muscles vibrate. This shakes the pollen out of the anthers onto the stigma.
105328.m: Bumblebees shake the pollen out of tomato flowers.

a: Pollen comes from another plant of the same species
Pollen comes from the same flower
The flower forms seeds without pollen
105329.e: In cross-pollination the pollen comes from another plant of the same species. In this way the genes of two plants are mixed.
105329.m: In cross-pollination the pollen comes from another plant.

105330.q: In cross-pollination, how does pollen get from one plant to another?
105330.e: Pollen cannot move by itself. Usually the wind or animals such as insects carry it to other plants.
105330.m: Wind and animals carry pollen to other plants.

105331.q: Why are different varieties of apple often planted next to each other in orchards?
a: Most varieties need pollen from another variety
105331.e: Most apple varieties hardly bear fruit if they are pollinated only with their own pollen. A suitable other variety nearby provides the pollen needed.
105331.m: Apple trees usually need pollen from another variety.

105332.q: How do many flowers prevent themselves from self-pollinating?
a: Stamens and stigma ripen at different times
105332.e: If the pollen is ripe before the stigma is ready to receive it, or the other way round, the plant’s own pollen hardly works. This encourages pollination by other plants.
105332.m: Pollen and stigma ripening at different times prevents self-pollination.

105333.q: In the willow, flowers with stamens and flowers with carpels grow on different plants. What is this called?
105333.e: In dioecious plants there are purely male and purely female plants. They always depend on cross-pollination.
105333.m: Dioecious plants have separate male and female plants.

105334.q: Pollen from which plant can usually fertilise a cherry blossom?
105334.e: Pollen only germinates on the stigma of a plant of the same or a very closely related species. Pollen from other species is not accepted.
105334.m: Fertilisation needs pollen from the same plant species.

105335.q: With which tool do plant breeders often transfer pollen to a stigma by hand?
105335.e: With a fine brush, pollen can be picked up carefully and dabbed onto the stigma. In this way breeders cross chosen plants.
105335.m: Breeders transfer pollen with a fine brush.

105336.q: Before a planned cross, what do breeders remove from the flower so that it does not pollinate itself?
105336.e: If the stamens are removed early, none of the flower’s own pollen can reach the stigma. Then the breeder adds the chosen pollen from another plant.
105336.m: Before a cross, the stamens of the flower are removed.

a: A group of flowers on one shoot
The place where a plant grows
The time when a plant flowers
105337.e: Many plants do not have single flowers but several flowers on a shared shoot. This group is called an inflorescence.
105337.m: An inflorescence is a group of flowers on one shoot.

105338.q: What are the bright red ‘petals’ of the poinsettia really?
105338.e: The red leaves of the poinsettia are coloured bracts. The real, small yellowish flowers sit in a cluster in their middle.
105338.m: In the poinsettia, bracts shine instead of petals.

105339.q: What is the inflorescence of the sunflower called, which looks like one single large flower?
105339.e: The sunflower belongs to the daisy family. Its ‘flower’ is a head made of hundreds of small single flowers.
105339.m: The sunflower is a head made of many small flowers.

105340.q: What are the white ‘petals’ around the edge of a daisy really?
105340.e: Each white ‘petal’ is a separate small flower, a ray floret. The disc florets sit in the yellow middle.
105340.m: The white rays of the daisy are single flowers.

105341.q: What do you call an inflorescence where all the flower stalks start from one point like the spokes of an umbrella?
105341.e: In an umbel all the flower stalks start at the same point. Ivy, for example, forms such an umbel.
105341.m: In an umbel all the flower stalks start from one point.

105342.q: What is an inflorescence with stalked flowers along a long axis called, as in lily of the valley?
105342.e: In a raceme, single flowers with stalks sit one after another on an unbranched main axis.
105342.m: A raceme has stalked flowers on a main axis.

105343.q: What do you call an inflorescence with stalkless flowers along an axis, as in ribwort plantain?
105343.e: In a spike the flowers sit directly on the main axis without their own stalk. In ribwort plantain it is short and cylinder-shaped.
105343.m: A spike has stalkless flowers on an axis.

105344.q: What inflorescence does the oat have, whose spikelets sit on branched, drooping stems?
105344.e: A panicle is a branched inflorescence whose branches get shorter towards the top. In oats the spikelets hang loosely from the branches.
105344.m: Oats carry their spikelets in a panicle.

105345.q: What is an inflorescence with a thick, fleshy axis called, like the one in lords-and-ladies?
105345.e: A spadix is a spike with a thickened axis. In lords-and-ladies it is surrounded by a hood-shaped bract.
105345.m: Lords-and-ladies carries its flowers on a spadix.

105346.q: What does a floral diagram show?
a: The arrangement of flower parts as a ground plan
The flowering time over the year
105346.e: A floral diagram is a simple ground plan of the flower seen from above. It shows the number and position of calyx, corolla, stamens and carpels.
105346.m: A floral diagram shows the flower as a simple ground plan.

105347.q: What is the short way of writing a flower with letters and numbers called, such as “K5 C5 A10 G1”?
105347.e: The floral formula sums up the structure of a flower in one line. Letters stand for the flower parts, numbers for how many there are.
105347.m: A floral formula describes a flower with letters and numbers.

105348.q: What does the letter K stand for in a floral formula?
105348.e: K stands for calyx, from the Greek word kalyx. The number after it shows how many sepals the flower has.
105348.m: In the floral formula K stands for the calyx.

105349.q: In a floral formula, what does the number after a letter tell you?
a: How many of those flower parts there are
105349.e: In a floral formula such as “K5 C5” the letter stands for a part of the flower. The number after it shows how many of them the flower has.
105349.m: The numbers in the floral formula give the number of flower parts.

105350.q: Which flower parts are drawn right in the middle of a floral diagram?
105350.e: The carpels with the ovary lie in the middle of the flower. That is why they are also in the centre of the floral diagram.
105350.m: In the floral diagram the carpels are in the middle.

105351.q: Which sign do you write in a floral formula when a flower has a great many stamens?
105351.e: When parts are too many to count, the floral formula uses the sign ∞. This is the case, for example, with the many stamens of the rose.
105351.m: For a great many flower parts you write the infinity sign.

105352.q: What must you do with a flower first in order to draw a floral diagram?
a: Measure the leaves on the stem
Describe the scent of the flower
105352.e: A floral diagram shows the number and position of calyx, corolla, stamens and carpels. That is why you first count these parts carefully.
105352.m: For a floral diagram you count the flower parts.

105353.q: How many planes of symmetry does a two-sided symmetrical flower, such as a pea flower, have?
105353.e: Two-sided symmetrical (zygomorphic) flowers can only be divided into mirror-image halves along a single plane.
105353.m: A zygomorphic flower has only one plane of symmetry.

105354.q: In which order are the flower parts arranged in a floral diagram from outside to inside?
105354.e: Right on the outside are the sepals, then come the petals and the stamens. The carpels sit in the middle.
105354.m: From outside to inside: calyx, corolla, stamens, carpels.

105355.q: Which computing term goes back to the name of the scholar Al-Khwarizmi?
105355.e: The Latin form of his name, “Algoritmi”, became the word algorithm. It means an exact sequence of steps for solving a task.
105355.m: The word algorithm comes from the name Al-Khwarizmi.

105356.q: Which branch of mathematics got its name from the title of a book by Al-Khwarizmi?
105356.e: In his book on calculating by “al-jabr” and “al-muqabala”, he solved equations. “Al-jabr” became the word algebra.
105356.m: The word algebra comes from the title of a book by Al-Khwarizmi.

105357.q: In which city did Al-Khwarizmi work at the famous “House of Wisdom”?
105357.e: The House of Wisdom in Baghdad was a centre for translation and research. Al-Khwarizmi worked there on behalf of the caliph.
105357.m: Al-Khwarizmi did research at the House of Wisdom in Baghdad.

105358.q: Which numerals did Al-Khwarizmi make known in the Arab world with a book on arithmetic?
105358.e: He described calculating with the numerals from India, including zero and place value. Through his book, this way of calculating spread in the Islamic world.
105358.m: Our numerals originally come from India.

105359.q: What do you learn in algebra, which goes back to Al-Khwarizmi?
105359.e: Al-Khwarizmi showed how to solve equations using fixed rules. The word “al-jabr”, meaning completion, became algebra.

105360.q: Which type of equation did Al-Khwarizmi solve systematically in his book?
105360.e: He showed step by step how to solve equations containing the square of the unknown. He also explained the solutions with geometric figures.
105360.m: Al-Khwarizmi solved quadratic equations using fixed rules.

105361.q: Who was Al-Ma'mun, who supported Al-Khwarizmi in Baghdad?
105361.e: Caliph al-Ma'mun supported science and translation in the early 9th century. Al-Khwarizmi dedicated his book on algebra to him.

105362.q: In which language did Ibn al-Haytham write his books?
105362.e: Ibn al-Haytham was a scholar of the Islamic world and wrote in Arabic. His works were later translated into Latin, where he was called Alhazen.

105363.q: What was Ibn al-Haytham's most famous book about?
105363.e: In his “Book of Optics” he studied how light travels and how we see. The work influenced science in Europe for centuries.
105363.m: Ibn al-Haytham studied light and vision.

105364.q: What did Ibn al-Haytham show about seeing?
a: Light falls from objects into the eye
The eye sends out rays of sight
105364.e: Many ancient scholars believed the eye sent out rays. Ibn al-Haytham showed that light comes from things and reaches the eye.
105364.m: We see because light from things falls into our eyes.

105365.q: Which device did Ibn al-Haytham describe, in which a small hole casts an upside-down image into a dark room?
105365.e: In a camera obscura, light falls through a small hole and creates an upside-down image on the wall. Ibn al-Haytham used it to study how light travels.
105365.m: The camera obscura makes an upside-down image through a hole.

105366.q: Which part of the world did Ibn al-Haytham come from?
105366.e: Ibn al-Haytham was born around 965 in Basra in present-day Iraq. Later he lived in Egypt.
105366.m: Ibn al-Haytham came from the Middle East.

105367.q: In which country with famous pyramids did Ibn al-Haytham later do his research?
105367.e: Ibn al-Haytham moved to Cairo in Egypt. There he wrote his most important works.
105367.m: Ibn al-Haytham later did research in Egypt.

105368.q: Why is Ibn al-Haytham regarded as a pioneer of modern science?
105368.e: Instead of simply accepting old teachings, he checked them with planned experiments and measurements. That is at the heart of the scientific method.
