106373.m: Aquaplaning happens when the tyre tread can no longer channel the water away.

106374.q: How is the risk of aquaplaning related to speed?
a: It does not depend on speed
It only exists when standing still
106374.e: The faster a car goes, the less time the tread has to push the water away. Driving more slowly is therefore the most important protection.
106374.m: In the wet, driving slowly protects against aquaplaning.

106375.q: Which tyres increase the risk of aquaplaning?
106375.e: The less tread a tyre has, the less water it can channel away. Worn tyres therefore ride up on the water much sooner.

106376.q: What should you do if the car starts aquaplaning?
a: Take your foot off the accelerator and keep the steering wheel straight
106376.e: As the car slows down, the tyres get contact with the road again. Steering or braking hard can then make the car skid.
106376.m: When aquaplaning, calmly ease off the accelerator and steer straight.

106377.q: Why does the car hardly respond to steering during aquaplaning?
a: There is hardly any friction left between tyre and road
106377.e: Steering only works if the tyres pass forces onto the road through static friction. On the film of water this grip is almost completely missing.
106377.m: Without static friction a car cannot be steered.

106378.q: Where on roads does a lot of water collect that can lead to aquaplaning?
106378.e: Ruts are dips that many heavy vehicles have pressed into the road surface. Rainwater stays in them.
106378.m: A dangerous amount of water can collect in ruts.

106379.q: What is often a sign that aquaplaning is starting?
a: The steering suddenly feels very light
106379.e: When the front wheels ride up on the water, you need almost no force to steer. Often the engine revs briefly rise too because the wheels spin.
106379.m: Suddenly light steering warns of aquaplaning.

106380.q: What does an anti-lock braking system, ABS for short, prevent in an emergency stop?
106380.e: The ABS briefly releases the brake on a wheel as soon as it is about to lock. This keeps the wheels turning while braking.
106380.m: ABS stops the wheels locking when braking.

106381.q: Why is it important that the wheels do not lock when braking?
a: Rolling wheels can still be steered
Locked wheels make the car faster
106381.e: A locked wheel slides and cannot pass on any sideways forces. With ABS you can steer round an obstacle even during an emergency stop.
106381.m: Thanks to ABS a car can still be steered in an emergency stop.

106382.q: Which driver assistance system uses the ABS sensors and stops the car skidding in bends?
106382.e: The electronic stability programme ESP is built on ABS. If the car threatens to break away, it brakes individual wheels in a targeted way.
106382.m: ESP helps against skidding and uses the ABS sensors to do so.

106383.q: How does the ABS detect that a wheel is about to lock?
a: With sensors that measure wheel speed
With a camera in the boot
From the sound of the engine
From the temperature of the seats
106383.e: On each wheel a speed sensor measures how fast it is turning. If one wheel suddenly slows down much more than the others, the ABS steps in.
106383.m: Wheel speed sensors tell the ABS when a wheel is locking.

106384.q: What can you often feel in the brake pedal when the ABS is working?
a: The pedal jumping up and staying there
106384.e: The ABS releases and applies the brake many times a second. You feel this as juddering in the pedal, but you should keep braking hard.
106384.m: If the brake pedal judders, the ABS is working and you keep braking.

106385.q: How common is ABS in new cars today?
a: It is only found in racing cars
It is only found in lorries
106385.e: ABS came onto the market at the end of the 1970s. Today practically all new cars have ABS fitted.
106385.m: ABS is standard in new cars today.

106386.q: Why is ABS especially helpful on a motorbike?
a: A locked front wheel easily leads to a fall
106386.e: If a motorbike's front wheel locks, the bike loses its stability and falls over. ABS prevents this and often shortens the braking distance.
106386.m: ABS protects motorcyclists from falling when braking.

106387.q: On which surface can the braking distance with ABS be longer than without?
a: On loose gravel or fresh snow
106387.e: On a loose surface a locked wheel pushes a braking wedge of material ahead of it. ABS prevents this wedge, but in return the car stays steerable.
106387.m: On loose surfaces ABS does not always brake shorter, but it keeps you steerable.

106388.q: Why do curlers sweep the ice in front of the stone?
a: The ice is warmed slightly and the stone slides further
They remove snow falling from the sky
106388.e: Sweeping warms the ice surface slightly, and a thin film of water reduces the friction. The stone then slides further and runs straighter.
106388.m: Sweeping reduces friction and lets the curling stone slide further.

106389.q: Why are fine drops of water sprayed onto the ice before curling and left to freeze?
a: The stone rests on only a few points and slides better
106389.e: The frozen droplets are called pebbles. The stone only touches their tips, so the friction is small.
106389.m: Frozen droplets help the curling stone slide better.

106390.q: Roughly how heavy is a curling stone?
106390.e: A curling stone may weigh at most just under 20 kg. Despite this weight it slides dozens of metres thanks to low friction.
106390.m: A curling stone weighs about 20 kilograms.

106391.q: What rock are curling stones made from?
106391.e: Curling stones are made of especially dense, hard granite. Many come from the Scottish island of Ailsa Craig.
106391.m: Curling stones are made of hard granite.

106392.q: What happens when a curling stone is released with a slight spin?
106392.e: A spinning stone drifts sideways on its way and follows a curve. The sport takes its name from this movement: to curl means to bend.
106392.m: A spinning curling stone travels in a curve.

106393.q: What part of a curling stone touches the ice?
a: A narrow ring on the underside
106393.e: The underside of the stone is slightly hollowed. It rests only on a narrow running ring, which keeps the friction small.
106393.m: A curling stone touches the ice only with a narrow ring.

106394.q: Which country does the sport of curling come from?
106394.e: Curling was played on frozen lakes in Scotland centuries ago. Later it spread to Canada and the Alpine countries.
106394.m: Curling has its origins in Scotland.

106395.q: How do curlers influence the path of the stone after it has been released?
a: With brooms they use to sweep the ice
With sticks they use to push the stone
106395.e: After release nobody may touch the stone. But sweeping with the broom makes it slide further and straighter.
106395.m: In curling you guide the stone with the broom.

106396.q: Why is glide wax put on the base of skis?
a: So that the skis glide better
So that the skis brake better
So that the skis get heavier
106396.e: Glide wax reduces sliding friction between ski and snow. It also protects the base from drying out.

106397.q: Which wax stops the ski slipping back when you push off in classic cross-country skiing?
106397.e: Grip wax is put on under the binding. When you push off it sticks briefly to the snow, yet when gliding it still lets the ski run forwards.
106397.m: In classic cross-country skiing, grip wax gives you hold when pushing off.

106398.q: Why is ski wax chosen to match the snow temperature?
a: Cold and warm snow rub differently against the base
Otherwise the wax melts away completely at once
The colour of the wax must match the snow
Only then does the ski stay dry
106398.e: Cold snow has sharp, hard crystals, and wet snow forms more water. For cold snow you use harder wax, for warm snow softer wax.
106398.m: Good ski wax matches the temperature of the snow.

106399.q: Which ski waxes have been banned in international ski racing since the 2023/24 season?
106399.e: Fluorine waxes contain fluorine compounds that break down very slowly and harm the environment and health. The International Ski Federation has therefore banned them in racing.
106399.m: Ski waxes containing fluorine are banned in racing.

106400.q: How is glide wax often applied to a ski?
a: Ironed in with a hot waxing iron
Painted on cold with a brush and washed off at once
Diluted with water and poured on
106400.e: The wax is melted with an iron and worked into the base. After it cools, the excess is scraped off and the base is brushed out.
106400.m: Glide wax is ironed hot into the ski base.

106401.q: What is the base on the underside of a ski usually made of?
106401.e: Ski bases are usually made of a special plastic. It glides well on snow and can absorb wax.
106401.m: Ski bases are made of plastic that absorbs wax.

106402.q: Why are fine grooves, a structure, ground into the ski base?
a: So that no suction effect forms in wet snow
So that the ski brakes in the cold
So that the ski is easier to carry
So that the wax does not stick
106402.e: In wet snow a film of water can literally suck the ski down. The grooves channel the water away and reduce this effect.
106402.m: Grooves in the ski base stop suction on wet snow.

106403.q: What do some cross-country skis use instead of grip wax to get a hold when pushing off?
a: Fish scales or skins under the binding
106403.e: Fish scales in the base or fitted skins grip the snow when pushing off. When gliding forwards they lie flat.
106403.m: Fish scales or skins replace grip wax in cross-country skiing.

106404.q: What does a freshly waxed ski do when gliding compared with an unwaxed one?
a: Less sliding friction and higher speed
More sliding friction and more grip
106404.e: The wax fills the fine pores of the base and makes it smoother. This lowers friction, and you glide faster on the same slope.
106404.m: A well-waxed ski glides faster than a dry one.

106405.q: Why do sparks fly when you grind steel on a fast-spinning grinding wheel?
a: Frictional heat makes tiny metal particles glow
The grinding wheel contains firework powder
The spinning sets the air alight
106405.e: The grinding wheel tears off small steel shavings and heats them strongly through friction. The glowing particles fly off as sparks and partly burn in the air.
106405.m: Grinding creates so much frictional heat that metal shavings glow.

106406.q: What makes a match catch fire?
a: Frictional heat on the striking surface
An electric spark from a battery
106406.e: Striking it on the striking surface creates so much heat that the chemicals in the head start to burn. Safety matches only light on the striking surface of the box.
106406.m: Frictional heat lights the head of a match.

106407.q: How could people in the Stone Age make fire using friction?
a: By spinning a wooden stick quickly in a wooden board
By rubbing two pieces of ice together
106407.e: With a fire drill you spin a wooden stick quickly in a hollow. The frictional heat makes fine wood dust glow.
106407.m: Frictional heat can make wood glow.

106408.q: Why do a car's brake discs get very hot after a long descent from a mountain pass?
a: The brakes turn kinetic energy into heat
The air gets warmer going downhill
106408.e: When braking, the brake pads rub against the discs. The car's kinetic energy is turned into heat, and the discs can become glowing hot.
106408.m: Brakes turn the energy of motion into heat.

106409.q: Why should you drive in a low gear on long descents from Swiss mountain passes?
a: So that the brakes do not overheat
So that the tank fills up
So that the tyres get colder
So that the car goes faster
106409.e: In a low gear the engine helps to brake. So the brakes have to absorb less frictional heat and do not lose their effect.
106409.m: Going downhill in a low gear spares the brakes.

106410.q: Why do skis glide so well on snow in the first place?
a: Frictional heat creates a thin film of water
106410.e: Gliding creates a little heat through friction. It melts a wafer-thin layer of snow, and the ski glides more easily on this film of water.
106410.m: A wafer-thin film of water lets skis glide on snow.

106411.q: Why can you get burnt if a rope slides quickly through your hands?
a: The friction creates a lot of heat on the skin
The rope is soaked in acid
The rope is always electrically charged
The skin freezes onto the rope
106411.e: The fast-sliding rope rubs hard against the skin. The frictional heat produced can injure the skin like a burn.
106411.m: A fast-sliding rope can burn the skin through frictional heat.

106412.q: Why does a drill bit get hot when drilling into metal?
a: Because of friction between the bit and the metal
Because of the current in the cable
Because the air in the hole is burning
106412.e: When drilling, the cutting edge rubs hard against the workpiece. The frictional heat can be so great that you have to cool it with cutting oil or coolant.
106412.m: Drilling produces a lot of heat through friction.

106413.q: What happens to the kinetic energy of a sledge that comes to a stop through friction?
a: It is stored in the snow as electricity
106413.e: Energy is never lost, it is only changed. Friction turns the kinetic energy into heat in the runners and the snow.
106413.m: Friction turns kinetic energy into heat; it does not vanish.

106414.q: What are snow chains on a car for?
a: They improve grip on snow and ice
They protect the tyres from stones
106414.e: With chains the wheels can pass much bigger driving and braking forces onto snow and ice. That is why they are often essential on snowy mountain roads.
106414.m: Snow chains give tyres grip on snow and ice.

106415.q: In Switzerland, what does a round blue sign showing a tyre with a chain round it mean?
a: Snow chains are for sale here
106415.e: Round blue signs give an instruction. From this sign onwards you may only continue with snow chains fitted.
106415.m: The blue snow chain sign makes snow chains compulsory.

106416.q: On which wheels do you fit snow chains?
a: Only ever on the spare wheel
Only on the wheels that are not driven
106416.e: The chains are mainly meant to get the driving force onto the road. That is why they belong on the driven wheels.
106416.m: Snow chains belong on the driving wheels.

106417.q: Why should you take snow chains off on a road clear of snow?
a: They damage the road and tyres, and the car slides more easily
They make the car too light
Otherwise they freeze onto the tyre
106417.e: On dry asphalt the chain links do not grip but hammer on the surface. This damages the road, chains and tyres, and braking can get worse.
106417.m: Take snow chains off on a road clear of snow.

106418.q: How do snow chains improve friction on ice?
a: The chain links press into the ice and interlock
They melt the ice with electricity
They scatter salt on the road
They lift the car off the ice
106418.e: The hard chain links press into the surface of the ice and snow. This creates an interlocking grip that passes on much more force than smooth rubber.
106418.m: Snow chains interlock with snow and ice.

106419.q: When is the best time to practise fitting snow chains?
a: At home, before you drive into the mountains
Not until a snowstorm on the pass
Never, you fit them while driving
Only in summer on the motorway
106419.e: In snow and cold, fitting unfamiliar chains is hard work. If you have practised beforehand, you are quicker and safer when it really matters.
106419.m: It is best to try fitting snow chains at home first.

106420.q: What are so-called snow socks for car tyres?
a: Fabric covers that improve grip as a light alternative to chains
106420.e: Snow socks are fabric covers pulled over the tyres. The fabric soaks up moisture and so improves grip on snow.
106420.m: Fabric snow socks are a light alternative to snow chains.

106421.q: Are good winter tyres enough on a road with the sign “snow chains compulsory”?
a: No, you still need snow chains
Yes, if they are less than a year old
Yes, but only during the day
106421.e: The sign applies whatever tyres you have. Even cars with good winter tyres must fit snow chains there.
106421.m: Where snow chains are compulsory, winter tyres alone are not enough.

106422.q: In ecology, what is meant by an altitude zone?
a: A height range with typical plant life
A measuring stick for snow depth
106422.e: As altitude increases, temperature and climate change. That is why in the mountains there are zones one above the other, each with typical plants and forests.
106422.m: Each altitude zone has its own typical plant life.

106423.q: Which order is correct in the Alps from bottom to top?
a: Broadleaved forest, conifer forest, alpine pastures, rock and ice
Conifer forest, broadleaved forest, rock and ice, alpine pastures
Alpine pastures, broadleaved forest, conifer forest, rock and ice
Rock and ice, alpine pastures, conifer forest, broadleaved forest
106423.e: Down in the warm hill country broadleaved forests grow, further up conifer forests. Above the tree line come alpine pastures and right at the top rock, snow and ice.
106423.m: From bottom to top: broadleaved forest, conifer forest, alpine pastures, rock and ice.

106424.q: Why are there altitude zones in the mountains at all?
a: Because it gets cooler with height
Because the air is damper higher up
Because more animals live higher up
Because the sun shines more weakly higher up
106424.e: With every metre of height the average temperature drops, and the growing season gets shorter. That is why only plants that cope well with cold can grow higher up.
106424.m: The drop in temperature with height is the main reason for altitude zones.

106426.q: What is typical of the highest altitude zone in the Alps?
106426.e: Right at the top the snow often stays all year round. Experts call this zone the nival zone, from the Latin word for snow. Only a few plants survive there.
106426.m: Snow and ice rule the highest altitude zone.

106427.q: Why are the altitude zones on south-facing slopes usually higher than on north-facing slopes?
a: South-facing slopes get more sun and warmth
There is no wind on north-facing slopes
106427.e: In Switzerland south-facing slopes face the sun more and are therefore warmer. Plants find good conditions there even at greater heights.
106427.m: On the sunny side the altitude zones reach further up.

106428.q: What happens to the growing season the higher you climb in the mountains?
106428.e: The growing season is the time of year when plants can grow. High up, spring starts later and winter earlier.
106428.m: The higher you go, the shorter the growing season for plants.

106429.q: What is the height line called above which the snow no longer melts away completely, even in summer?
106429.e: Above this line more snow falls in a year than can melt in summer. Firn and glaciers can form there.
106429.m: Above the snow line the snow stays all year round.

106430.q: People talk about the ‘aspect’ of a slope. What does that mean?
a: How many trees grow on it
106430.e: Whether a slope faces south or north decides how much sun it gets. This strongly affects temperature, snow cover and plant life.
106430.m: The aspect of a slope affects its plant life.

106431.e: The word comes from the Latin ‘collis’ for hill. The colline zone is the lowest and warmest altitude zone.
106431.m: The colline zone is the zone of the hill country.

106432.q: Where is the colline zone compared with the other altitude zones?
a: Right at the bottom, in the lowest areas
Right at the top by the glaciers
In the middle of the high mountains
106432.e: The colline zone is the lowest altitude zone. On the northern side of the Alps it reaches up to about 600 metres above sea level.
106432.m: The colline zone is the lowest altitude zone.

106433.q: Which crop is typical of sunny slopes in the colline zone in Switzerland?
106433.e: The vine needs a lot of warmth and a long summer. That is why vineyards such as those in Lavaux or Valais lie mainly in low, sunny places.
106433.m: Vineyards show typical places of the colline zone.

106434.q: Which kind of tree shapes many dry, warm forests of the colline zone?
106434.e: In warm, dry places such as Valais or the southern foot of the Jura, oak forests grow, for example with the downy oak. They cope well with heat and drought.
106434.m: Oaks love the warm places of the colline zone.

106435.q: Which type of tree naturally shapes the forests of the colline zone?
106435.e: At low altitudes the summers are long and warm, which suits broadleaved trees such as oak, lime and maple. Conifers are naturally rare there.
106435.m: Broadleaved forests naturally dominate the colline zone.

106436.q: Why is only a little natural forest left in the colline zone today?
a: People use it heavily for towns and farming
The ground there is too rocky
106436.e: The warm, flat areas are good for living in and for fields, fruit growing and vineyards. That is why a lot of forest was cleared there early on.
106436.m: The colline zone is strongly shaped by people.

106437.q: Where is the lowest point in Switzerland, a place in the colline zone?
106437.e: Lake Maggiore lies at about 193 metres above sea level, which makes it the lowest point in Switzerland. Even palms and camellias grow there.
106437.m: The lowest point in Switzerland is at Lake Maggiore.

106438.q: Which altitude zone comes directly above the colline zone in the mountains?
106438.e: Above the warm hill country comes the montane zone with mountain forests. After that come the subalpine, the alpine and, at the very top, the nival zone.
106438.m: The montane zone lies above the colline zone.

106439.q: What is the climate like in the colline zone compared with higher places?
a: Warmer, with a longer growing season
Exactly the same as in the high mountains
106439.e: At low altitudes the summers are long and warm and the winters mild. That is why broadleaved forests, fruit trees and vines grow well here.
106439.m: The colline zone is the warmest altitude zone.

106440.q: Where does the term ‘montane’ come from?
a: From the Latin word for mountain
From the Latin word for water
From the Greek word for forest
From the French word for meadow
106440.e: The Latin ‘mons, montis’ means mountain. The montane zone is the mountain forest zone above the hill country.
106440.m: The montane zone is the zone of mountain forests.

106441.q: Roughly what height range does the montane zone cover on the northern side of the Alps?
106441.e: The montane zone follows on from the colline zone. Depending on the region it reaches up to about 1400 metres, and a bit higher in the Central Alps because of the warmer climate.
106441.m: On the northern side of the Alps the montane zone starts at about 600 metres.

106442.q: Which two tree species shape many natural forests of the montane zone in the Alpine foothills?
106442.e: In the damp, fairly cool montane zone, beech and silver fir grow especially well together. Higher up, the spruce joins them.
106442.m: Beech and fir are the typical trees of the montane zone.

106443.q: What kind of farming is typical in the montane zone?
a: Meadows and pastures with dairy farming
106443.e: At this height it is too cool and wet for many field crops. But grass grows well, so mainly cows are kept there.
106443.m: Meadows, pastures and dairy farming dominate the montane zone.

106444.q: What are the typical pastures in the Jura called, where trees stand loosely scattered?
106444.e: Wooded pastures, in French ‘pâturages boisés’, combine forest and pasture on the same land. They shape the landscape of the Jura in the montane zone.
106444.m: Wooded pastures in the Jura are pastures with scattered trees.

106445.q: Which altitude zone covers most of the slopes in the Swiss Alpine foothills and the Jura?
106445.e: Many foothills, such as in the Emmental or Toggenburg, and the Jura heights lie between about 600 and 1400 metres. That matches the mountain forest zone.
106445.m: The Alpine foothills and the Jura lie mostly in the montane zone.

106446.q: Which tree species often joins beech and fir in the upper montane zone?
106446.e: The higher and cooler it gets, the better the spruce can compete. In the upper montane zone it often forms mixed forests with fir and beech.
106446.m: Further up in the montane zone the spruce joins in.

106447.q: Which statement about the climate of the montane zone is true?
a: It is cooler and wetter than on the Swiss Plateau
It is warmer and drier than on the Swiss Plateau
There is snow there all year round
106447.e: As altitude increases, temperatures drop, and clouds drop more rain on the mountains. That is why the montane zone is cooler and wetter.
106447.m: The montane zone is cooler and damper than the lowlands.

106448.q: Which altitude zone lies just below the tree line?
106448.e: The subalpine zone is the highest zone in which forest still grows. Above it comes the treeless alpine zone.
106448.m: The subalpine zone is the highest forest zone.

106449.q: What does the prefix ‘sub’ in ‘subalpine’ mean?
106449.e: ‘Sub’ is Latin and means ‘below’. So the subalpine zone lies below the alpine zone.
106449.m: Subalpine means below the alpine zone.

106450.q: Which conifer species forms most of the forests in the subalpine zone of the northern Alps?
106450.e: The spruce copes well with long, cold winters and grows even when the summer is short. That is why it shapes the subalpine forests in the northern Alps.
106450.m: Spruce dominates the subalpine zone of the northern Alps.

106451.q: Roughly how long is the growing season in the subalpine zone compared with the Swiss Plateau?
106451.e: High up, snow stays on the ground until spring, and it gets cold again in autumn. That is why trees grow only slowly there.
106451.m: In the subalpine zone trees grow slowly because of the short summers.

106452.q: Why do spruces in the subalpine zone often have narrow, pointed crowns?
a: So that snow slides off more easily
So that they produce more fruit
So that birds do not nest there
So that they lose their leaves in winter
106452.e: Heavy snow can break branches and trunks. A slim crown holds less snow and can bear the weight better.
106452.m: Slim crowns protect mountain spruces from snow damage.

106453.q: What is a grazing level between the valley and the alpine pasture called, which is used in spring and autumn?
106453.e: A Maiensäss lies between the farm in the valley and the actual alpine pasture. The cattle graze there in spring before moving further up in summer.
106453.m: On the Maiensäss the cattle graze before and after the alpine summer.

106454.q: Why do trees at the tree line often grow in small, dense groups?
a: They protect each other from snow, wind and cold
Because only then can they produce fruit
Because foresters have to plant them like that
So that cows cannot get through
106454.e: The climate in the subalpine zone is harsh. Trees in groups protect each other from snow, wind and cold.
106454.m: In the subalpine zone trees often grow in protective groups.

106455.q: Which large, rare bird of the grouse family lives in open conifer forests of the montane and subalpine zones?
106455.e: The capercaillie needs open, quiet mountain forests with lots of berry bushes on the ground. In Switzerland it has become rare and is strictly protected.
106455.m: The capercaillie is a rare inhabitant of open mountain forests.

106456.q: What is meant by the forest line?
a: The upper limit of closed forest
The edge of a forest by a lake
The boundary of a nature park
106456.e: Above the forest line the trees no longer stand close enough together to form a forest. Higher up there are only single trees.
106456.m: The forest line is the height above which no closed forest grows.

106457.q: What is the line called up to which single upright trees still grow?
106457.e: The tree line lies a little above the forest line. Between the two lines is a transition zone with scattered trees.
106457.m: The tree line lies above the forest line.

106458.q: At roughly what height is the forest line in the northern Swiss Alps?
106458.e: In the damper, cooler northern Alps the forest ends at about 1800 metres. In the Central Alps the limit is much higher.
106458.m: In the northern Alps the forest line is at about 1800 metres.

106459.q: Where in Switzerland is the forest line highest, at about 2300 m?
a: In the Central Alps such as Valais and the Engadine
106459.e: In the large, high mountain ranges of the Central Alps it is warmer and sunnier in summer. That is why the forest can climb higher there.
106459.m: In Valais and the Engadine the forest climbs especially high.

106460.q: What mainly limits tree growth at the forest line?
a: Temperatures that are too low in summer
106460.e: Trees need a minimum amount of warmth during the growing season to form new wood. As a rule of thumb, the forest line is where the warmest month reaches about 10 °C on average.
106460.m: The forest line is mainly set by a lack of summer warmth.

106461.q: What do you call the transition area at the forest line with stunted trees standing on their own?
106461.e: Here the trees struggle against cold, wind, snow and frost drought. Many grow low, crooked or only on one side.
106461.m: In the struggle zone trees only survive in harsh conditions.

106462.q: What can be seen at the forest line in many places in the Alps today?
a: The forest is slowly growing higher up
The forest is dying off completely
The forest line drops by 100 m every year
The trees are losing their needles for ever
106462.e: Warmer summers and fewer alpine pastures being farmed let young trees grow further up. This process is slow but measurable.
106462.m: With warming and less grazing, the forest is moving upwards.

106463.q: Which low conifer often forms dense, creeping thickets at the forest line?
106463.e: The dwarf mountain pine is a low-lying form of the mountain pine. Its flexible branches are pressed down by the snow but do not break.
106463.m: The dwarf mountain pine grows as crooked scrub at the forest line.

106464.q: Which type of forest would mostly grow on the Swiss Plateau without people?
106464.e: The climate and soils of the Swiss Plateau suit the beech very well. It competes so strongly there that it would push out most other tree species.
106464.m: Naturally, the Swiss Plateau would be beech forest country.

106465.q: What does the beech cope with badly?
106465.e: The beech needs well-aired soils. That is why other trees, such as alders or willows, grow in wet hollows and river floodplains.
106465.m: Beeches avoid wet soils and flood areas.

106466.q: Which Swiss forests have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2021?
a: Stone pine forests in the Engadine
106466.e: In 2021 UNESCO added beech forests on the Bettlachstock in the canton of Solothurn and in Ticino to the World Heritage Site ‘Ancient Beech Forests of Europe’. They are regarded as especially close to nature.
106466.m: Ancient Swiss beech forests are a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

106467.q: What do you call a beech forest with tall, smooth trunks and hardly any undergrowth?
106467.e: The trunks stand like pillars in a great hall, and the canopy forms the ceiling. Little grows on the ground because of the shade.
106467.m: A dense beech forest looks like a hall of pillars.

106468.q: Which special flowers can you find in open beech forests on dry limestone slopes in the Jura?
106468.e: On warm, chalky slopes the beech forest is more open than usual. Helleborines and other protected orchid species grow there, for example.
106468.m: Wild orchids flower in open beech forests on limestone.

106469.q: What happened to many beeches in northern Switzerland in the very dry summer of 2018?
a: Their leaves changed colour already in summer
They had twice as many leaves
106469.e: Because of the long drought, many beeches suffered from lack of water. Their leaves turned brown already in midsummer and some fell off.
106469.m: Drought is also very hard on the beech.

106470.q: Up to roughly what height does the beech grow in the northern Swiss Alps?
106470.e: The beech is a tree of low and middle altitudes. Further up, the winters are too long and late frosts too frequent for it.
106470.m: In the northern Alps the beech grows up to about 1500 metres.

106471.q: Which large woodpecker especially likes to carve its nest holes in old beeches?
106471.e: The thick, smooth trunks of old beeches are good for large holes. Abandoned black woodpecker holes are later used by stock doves, bats and owls too.
106471.m: The black woodpecker likes to build its holes in old beeches.

106472.q: Which tree species of the fir and beech forest is browsed especially heavily by roe deer and red deer?
106472.e: Deer love the buds and shoots of young firs. Where there are too many deer, young firs are often missing, and the forest gradually loses this tree species.
106472.m: Young silver firs suffer especially badly from browsing by deer.

106473.q: What makes the silver fir especially valuable for mixed forests?
a: It can grow up even in deep shade
It drops all its needles in winter
It needs full sun to germinate
106473.e: Young firs can wait for decades in the shade of old trees. As soon as light falls through a gap, they grow quickly.
106473.m: The silver fir is a true shade-tolerant tree.

106474.q: Which third tree species is often mixed in with fir and beech in the fir and beech forest?
106474.e: The sycamore thrives in the damp, nutrient-rich soils of mountain forests. It often grows together with fir and beech.
106474.m: The sycamore often joins the fir and beech forest.

106475.q: In which regions of Switzerland is the fir and beech forest especially widespread?
a: In the Jura and the Alpine foothills
In the Engadine and Upper Valais
106475.e: The Jura and the Alpine foothills offer a damp, fairly cool climate at middle altitudes. There, silver fir and beech grow especially well together.
106475.m: The fir and beech forest shapes the Jura and the Alpine foothills.

106476.q: What harmed many silver firs in Switzerland in the 1980s?
106476.e: At that time many trees, especially silver firs, lost needles because of air pollution. People talked about ‘forest dieback’. Since then the air has become much cleaner.
106476.m: Dirty air harmed many silver firs in the 1980s.

106477.q: Why is the silver fir seen as an important tree species for the future in Switzerland?
a: It copes with drought better than the spruce
It only grows in the high mountains
It loses its needles in summer
106477.e: Thanks to its deep roots, the fir can still reach water even in dry summers. That is why foresters are relying on it more and more as the climate changes.
106477.m: The silver fir copes with climate change better than the spruce.

106478.q: What is special about silver fir wood?
106478.e: Unlike spruce, pine or larch, fir wood has no resin canals. That is why it is good for barrels, wall panelling and building parts that should not leak resin.
106478.m: Fir wood contains hardly any resin.

106479.q: Which scented plant with whorled leaves often grows on the floor of beech and fir and beech forests?
106479.e: Sweet woodruff forms small carpets in shady mixed broadleaved forests. Its leaves stand in a star around the stem and smell of hay when dried.
106479.m: Sweet woodruff grows in the shade of beeches and firs.

106480.q: What is the wood of slow-growing mountain spruces especially sought after for?
a: For floors in indoor swimming pools
For garden fences in the sea
106480.e: Spruces from high, cold places have very even, narrow growth rings. This tonewood vibrates well and is valued in instrument making, for example from the Risoud forest in the Jura.
106480.m: Mountain spruces provide valuable tonewood for instruments.

106481.q: Why are spruces increasingly at risk in low, warm areas of the Swiss Plateau?
a: They suffer from heat and drought
The ground there is too cold
106481.e: The spruce is really a tree of cool mountain forests. In warm lowlands, planted spruces get stressed in droughts and become vulnerable to pests.
106481.m: In warm lowlands the spruce is at a disadvantage with climate change.

106482.q: Which bird with crossed beak tips gets the seeds out of spruce cones?
106482.e: With its crossed beak it prises the cone scales apart. It even breeds in winter if there are enough cones.
106482.m: The common crossbill specialises in spruce seeds.

106483.q: Which dwarf shrub shapes the undergrowth of many acidic subalpine spruce forests?
106483.e: The bilberry loves acidic, humus-rich soils and light shade. That is why it often forms dense carpets in mountain spruce forests.
106483.m: Bilberries often grow on the ground in mountain spruce forests.

106484.q: What does fallen spruce needle litter do to the soil over time?
a: It makes the soil more acidic
It has no effect at all
106484.e: Spruce needles break down only slowly and form an acidic layer of humus. Many plants and soil animals do not like such soils.
106484.m: Spruce needles make the forest soil acidic.

106485.q: Roughly how tall can spruces grow?
106485.e: Spruces usually reach 30 to 50 metres, and single trees a little more. This makes them some of the tallest trees in Europe.
106485.m: Spruces can grow about 50 metres tall.

106486.q: What do you call a forest where almost only spruces of the same age have been planted over a large area?
106486.e: In the past, pure spruce stands were often planted on the Swiss Plateau because the spruce grows fast. But such monocultures are vulnerable to storms, drought and pests.
106486.m: Spruce monocultures grow fast but are vulnerable.

106487.q: Why is it rather dark all year round on the floor of a dense spruce forest?
a: Spruces keep their needles even in winter
Spruces lose all their needles in autumn
Spruce forests always stand in gorges
106487.e: As evergreen trees, spruces keep their dense canopy all year. Unlike in a broadleaved forest, there is no bright period in spring.
106487.m: A dense spruce forest is shady all year round.

106488.q: In which areas of Switzerland are larch and stone pine forests especially widespread?
106488.e: Larch and stone pine forests love the dry climate of the inner Alpine valleys with cold winters and lots of sun. The spruce does less well there.
106488.m: In the Engadine and Valais larches and stone pines shape the mountain forests.

106489.q: Which well-known forest at Riederalp is an old larch and stone pine forest?
106489.e: The Aletsch Forest lies above the Great Aletsch Glacier in Valais. It is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site Swiss Alps Jungfrau-Aletsch.
106489.m: The Aletsch Forest is a famous stone pine and larch forest in Valais.

106490.q: Why does a lot of grass and herbs often grow under larches, so that cattle can graze there?
a: The open larch crown lets a lot of light through
Larches fertilise the soil with sugar
106490.e: Larches have a loose crown with fine needles. The light reaches the ground, which is why grazed larch meadows form in the mountains.
106490.m: Larch forests are open and let grass grow.

106491.q: Which tree of the larch and stone pine forest is usually the first to settle open areas such as avalanche tracks or land in front of glaciers?
106491.e: The larch needs a lot of light and grows fast when young. As a pioneer tree it conquers open ground, while the stone pine follows later.
106491.m: The larch is a typical pioneer tree of the Alps.

106492.q: How fast does the Swiss stone pine grow?
a: Only in its first two years
106492.e: High up, the growing season is short, and the stone pine adds only a little wood each year. That is why its wood has very narrow growth rings.
106492.m: The Swiss stone pine grows very slowly.

106493.q: Why is the larch well protected from drying out in winter?
a: Without needles it loses hardly any water
It stores water in its cones
It drinks snow through its bark
106493.e: When the ground is frozen, trees cannot take up more water. Evergreen trees still lose water through their needles, but the bare larch hardly does.
106493.m: The bare larch is protected from frost drought.

106494.q: Which moth regularly eats whole larch forests brown in the Engadine?
106494.e: The caterpillars of this moth multiply in huge numbers about every eight to ten years and eat the needles. The larches usually grow new needles afterwards.
106494.m: The larch bud moth turns larch forests brown in some years.

106495.q: Roughly how tall can larches grow?
106495.e: Larches usually grow 30 to 40 metres tall. High up at the forest line, though, they often stay much smaller because of the harsh climate.
106495.m: Larches can grow about 40 metres tall.

106496.q: What is typical of a floodplain forest?
a: It is regularly flooded by a river
106496.e: Floodplain forests lie along rivers and streams whose water level changes a lot. In floods they are under water, and afterwards they dry out again.
106496.m: Floodplain forests live with regular flooding.

106499.q: Roughly what share of Switzerland’s floodplains has disappeared over time?
106499.e: Rivers were straightened and walled in, and floodplains were drained and built on. Only a small remnant of the original floodplains is left.
106499.m: Most of Switzerland’s floodplains have disappeared.

106500.q: Roughly how much of Switzerland’s land area do floodplains still cover today?
106500.e: Floodplains have shrunk to a very small part of the country’s area. Even so, they are home to a huge variety of living things.
106500.m: Floodplains cover only a tiny part of Switzerland.

106501.q: Why are floodplains seen as habitats especially rich in species?
a: There is never any water there
A lot of fertiliser is used there
Only a few plants grow there
106501.e: Floods drop gravel and sand, tear open banks and form new ponds. This creates an ever-changing patchwork in which about half of all Swiss plant species are found.
106501.m: The movement of the water makes floodplains so rich in species.

106503.q: What does the Confederation protect with the Federal Inventory of Floodplains of National Importance?
a: The most valuable floodplains in Switzerland
106503.e: Since 1992, especially valuable floodplains have been protected by the Confederation. The inventory now includes more than 300 areas.
106503.m: The Confederation protects the most important floodplains in Switzerland.

106504.q: Roughly what share of Swiss forest has a protective function?
106504.e: According to federal surveys, about half of the Swiss forest area counts as protection forest. The share is especially large in the Alpine cantons.
106504.m: About half of Swiss forest is protection forest.

106505.q: How does a forest protect against avalanches?
a: The trees hold the snow in place
The trees blow the snow away
106505.e: The many tree trunks hold the snow in place on the slope. So it cannot slide down as a big avalanche.
106505.m: Trees hold the snow in place on the slope.

106506.q: How does a forest protect against falling rocks?
a: The trunks slow down and stop falling rocks
106506.e: A falling rock hits trunks and loses energy. In this way a dense, healthy forest with many trunks holds back a lot of rocks.
106506.m: Tree trunks act as a brake against falling rocks.

106507.q: Why is looking after protection forest often cheaper than technical protective structures?
a: A well-kept forest protects for a long time at much lower cost
106507.e: Avalanche barriers and rockfall nets are expensive to build and maintain. A protection forest that is looked after does its job year after year for a fraction of that.
106507.m: A well-kept protection forest is cheap protection.

106508.q: What is a ‘Bannwald’, like the one Andermatt already had in the Middle Ages?
a: A forest where felling was banned so it would protect against avalanches
A forest where only the king was allowed to hunt
A forest that was burnt to gain grazing land
A forest where criminals were abandoned
106508.e: With a written ban, the valley people forbade the use of the forest above the village. So it stayed dense and protected Andermatt from avalanches. The protected forest of Andermatt is still well known today.
106508.m: A Bannwald could not be cut down because it protected against avalanches.

106509.q: Which animals threaten the young trees in protection forest when their numbers are too high?
a: Red deer, roe deer and chamois
106509.e: These plant-eaters eat the buds and shoots of young trees. Without young trees, the protection forest cannot keep doing its job in the long run.
106509.m: Too many deer can stop the protection forest from renewing itself.

106510.q: How does a forest help against landslides and erosion on steep slopes?
a: The roots hold the soil together
The crowns make the soil heavier
The bark draws water out of the rock
106510.e: A dense network of roots anchors the soil like a net. The forest floor also stores a lot of rainwater and releases it slowly.
106510.m: Roots hold the soil in place on the slope.

106511.q: What is built above the forest so that the snow cover there does not slide off as an avalanche?
106511.e: Snow supporting structures made of steel or wood hold the snow cover in place on steep slopes. Up there they do the job that the forest does further down.
106511.m: Snow supporting structures replace the forest where none grows.

106512.q: Why does a protection forest need to be looked after regularly?
a: So that young trees always grow up
So that it stays as dark as possible
So that it does not grow roots
So that no animals live there
106512.e: If a forest has only trees of the same age, many can collapse at the same time. That is why foresters create gaps where young trees can grow.
106512.m: A protection forest needs trees of every age.

106513.q: What is typical of a selection forest?
a: Trees of all ages grow side by side
All the trees are the same age
There is only a single layer of trees
106513.e: In a selection forest, small, medium and large trees grow closely mixed on the same area. This creates a layered structure from the ground up to the crowns.
106513.m: In a selection forest young and old trees stand side by side.

106514.q: How is a selection forest used?
a: The whole forest is felled at once
106514.e: The forester keeps removing single trees that are mature or in the way. This keeps the forest closed all the time and renewing itself constantly.
106514.m: In a selection forest only single trees are removed.

106515.q: Which tree species make up the classic Swiss selection forests?
a: Stone pine, larch and dwarf mountain pine
106515.e: These three tree species can survive as young trees in the shade of the big ones. This is what makes it possible for all ages to grow side by side.
106515.m: Fir, spruce and beech make up the typical selection forest.

106516.q: Which Swiss region is regarded as classic selection forest country?
106516.e: The farmers’ forests in the Emmental have been managed by selection for generations. Some of the most impressive selection forests in Europe stand there.
106516.m: The Emmental is known for its selection forests.

106517.q: What does a forester in a selection forest measure regularly to know how much wood can be harvested?
106517.e: The Neuchâtel forester Henri Biolley measured the stock of timber regularly. So he harvested only as much as grew back.
106517.m: In a selection forest only as much wood is harvested as grows back.

106518.q: Which way of harvesting wood is basically banned in Swiss forests?
106518.e: The federal Forest Act bans clear-cutting, where large areas are felled all at once. The forest is meant to stay natural and last.

106519.q: Why is a selection forest good as a protection forest?
a: It is always closed and never has big gaps
It consists only of broadleaved trees
It only grows in the lowlands
106519.e: Because only single trees are ever missing, the ground stays covered by forest all the time. So the forest can do its protective job without a break.
106519.m: A selection forest protects all the time because it never becomes bare.

106520.q: What must young trees in a selection forest above all be able to cope with?
106520.e: Only a little light gets through the canopy of the big trees. Young trees there have to wait a long time until a gap opens.
106520.m: Young trees in a selection forest grow up in the shade.

106547.q: In which subject did Emmy Noether become famous?
106547.e: Emmy Noether is considered one of the most important women mathematicians in history. Her work shaped algebra in particular.
106547.m: Emmy Noether was a great mathematician.

106548.q: In which natural science is Emmy Noether’s famous theorem from 1918 still a cornerstone today?
106548.e: Her theorem links symmetries with quantities that are conserved, such as energy. It is a cornerstone of modern physics.
106548.m: Emmy Noether’s theorem is very important for physics.

106549.q: What does the conservation of energy, which follows from Emmy Noether’s theorem, say?
a: Energy is not lost, it is only changed into another form
Energy gets less and less over time
Energy appears by itself out of nothing
106549.e: Noether showed that the conservation of energy follows from the fact that the laws of nature apply today just as they will tomorrow. Energy can only change from one form into another.
106549.m: Energy is never lost, it is only changed into another form.

106550.q: In which country did Emmy Noether do research and teach before she had to flee in 1933?
106550.e: Emmy Noether worked at the University of Göttingen, which was then a centre of mathematics. In 1933 she was dismissed by the Nazis.
106550.m: Emmy Noether did her research in Göttingen.

106551.q: How was Emmy Noether at first able to give lectures in Göttingen, even though women were not allowed to qualify as professors?
a: They were announced under a professor’s name
She taught disguised as a man
She only gave them in a café
She only sent them out as letters
106551.e: As a woman, she was at first not allowed her own licence to teach. So David Hilbert advertised the courses under his name, but Noether taught them.
106551.m: Noether’s first lectures ran under the name of a colleague.

106552.q: Why was Emmy Noether not allowed to teach officially at the university for a long time?
a: Because she did not speak German
106552.e: At that time women in Germany were not allowed to gain the qualification needed to become a professor. Only in 1919 did Noether get permission to teach officially.
106552.m: Emmy Noether gained her teaching qualification in 1919.

106553.q: Where did Emmy Noether emigrate to after the Nazis dismissed her in 1933?
106553.e: Because she was of Jewish descent, she lost her job. She found a new post at Bryn Mawr College in Pennsylvania.
106553.m: Emmy Noether had to emigrate to the USA in 1933.

106554.q: Which branch of mathematics did Emmy Noether shape particularly strongly?
106554.e: She studied general structures such as rings and ideals. Terms like “Noetherian ring” still bear her name today.
106554.m: Emmy Noether is seen as the mother of modern algebra.

106555.q: What first made Hedy Lamarr world-famous?
a: Being a film actress in Hollywood
106555.e: Hedy Lamarr acted in many Hollywood films and was considered a big star. For a long time only a few people knew that she was also an inventor.
106555.m: Hedy Lamarr was first known as a film star.

106556.q: What was Hedy Lamarr besides being an actress?
106556.e: During the Second World War, Hedy Lamarr developed an important idea for radio technology. For a long time hardly anyone knew about it.
106556.m: Hedy Lamarr was an actress and an inventor.

106557.q: What is the method that Hedy Lamarr invented called?
106557.e: With this method, the transmitter and receiver keep switching radio frequency at the same time. This makes it hard to listen in on the signal or to jam it.

106558.q: What was Hedy Lamarr’s invention originally meant for in the Second World War?
a: Radio control of torpedoes that could not be jammed
106558.e: Enemies were not supposed to be able to jam the radio signals used for steering. However, the US Navy did not use the idea at that time.
106558.m: Lamarr’s invention was first intended for torpedoes.

106559.q: How many frequencies did Hedy Lamarr’s patent use, matching the keys of a piano?
106559.e: A normal piano has 88 keys. As in a self-playing piano, punched paper strips were meant to control the switching.

106560.q: Which modern technology is based on ideas similar to Hedy Lamarr’s invention?
106560.e: Bluetooth devices switch their radio channels many hundreds of times per second. This way, lots of devices interfere with each other less.
106560.m: Bluetooth uses the idea of frequency hopping.

106561.q: Why is Inventors’ Day celebrated on 9 November in Germany, Austria and Switzerland?
a: The wheel was invented on that day
It is the day Edison died
It is the day of the first Moon landing
106561.e: The day remembers the actress and inventor. It is meant to show how important inventions are for society.
106561.m: Inventors’ Day is Hedy Lamarr’s birthday.

106562.q: Which animals did Dian Fossey study?
106562.e: Dian Fossey lived for years close to these large apes. She closely observed their family life and behaviour.

106563.q: In which African country did Dian Fossey set up her research station in 1967?
106563.e: The station lies in the Virunga volcanoes, where the mountain gorillas live in mountain forests. Fossey spent almost twenty years there.
106563.m: Dian Fossey did her research in Rwanda.

106564.q: Where was Dian Fossey’s research station Karisoke?
a: In the middle of a big city
106564.e: The station was in Rwanda between the volcanoes Karisimbi and Visoke. The mountain gorillas live there in misty mountain forests.
106564.m: Dian Fossey’s station was in the mountain forests of Rwanda.

106565.q: What is the name of Dian Fossey’s well-known book, which was also made into a film in 1988?
106565.e: In the book she describes her life with the gorillas. In the film, Sigourney Weaver played the scientist.
106565.m: “Gorillas in the Mist” tells the story of Dian Fossey’s life.

106566.q: Who did Dian Fossey fight against particularly determinedly?
106566.e: Poachers set traps and killed gorillas. Fossey destroyed traps and campaigned for strict protection.

106567.q: What happened in 1977 to Digit, Dian Fossey’s favourite gorilla?
a: He was taken to a zoo
He became leader of the group
106567.e: His death deeply shocked Fossey. Afterwards she set up a fund to protect the gorillas better.
106567.m: The death of the gorilla Digit made Fossey a fighter against poachers.

106568.q: How did Dian Fossey get the shy gorillas used to having her nearby?
a: She copied their behaviour and their sounds
106568.e: Fossey crouched down, chewed on plants and imitated gorilla sounds. In this way the animals slowly lost their fear.
106568.m: Dian Fossey copied the gorillas to win their trust.

106569.q: Which apes did Biruté Galdikas study on Borneo?
106569.e: Galdikas began her research in Indonesia in the 1970s. Together with Dian Fossey and Jane Goodall she forms a famous trio of women scientists.

106570.q: Which plant did Barbara McClintock do research on all her life?
106570.e: She studied the colourfully speckled kernels on cobs of maize. From them she drew conclusions about heredity.
106570.m: Barbara McClintock studied the genetics of maize.

a: Genes that can change their place in the genetic material
106571.e: She realised that certain sections of the genetic material jump and can switch other genes on or off. They are called transposons.

106572.q: What are the movable sections of genetic material discovered by McClintock commonly called?
106572.e: Experts call them transposons. They have their popular name because they change their position in the genetic material.
106572.m: Transposons are also called jumping genes.

106573.q: What did McClintock explain in maize with her movable genes?
a: The colourful spots on the kernels
106573.e: If such an element jumps into a colour gene or back out again, the colour of individual cells changes. This produces speckled kernels.
106573.m: Movable genes explain speckled maize kernels.

106574.q: In which year did Barbara McClintock receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine?
106574.e: She received the prize around three decades after her discovery. For a long time many experts had not taken her ideas seriously.
106574.m: McClintock received the Nobel Prize in 1983.

106575.q: What was special about Barbara McClintock’s Nobel Prize?
a: She was the first woman to receive the Nobel Prize in Medicine on her own
She shared it with five people
106575.e: Earlier women winners in this field had shared the prize with others. McClintock was the only person honoured.
106575.m: Barbara McClintock received the Nobel Prize in Medicine unshared.

106576.q: Which country did Barbara McClintock come from?
106576.e: She was born in Connecticut in 1902 and studied at Cornell University. Later she did research for a long time in the laboratory at Cold Spring Harbor near New York.
106576.m: Barbara McClintock was an American geneticist.

106577.q: With which instrument did Barbara McClintock study the chromosomes of maize?
106577.e: Chromosomes are tiny. McClintock stained them and looked at them under the microscope to spot changes.
106577.m: McClintock studied chromosomes under the microscope.

106578.q: For which organisation did Katherine Johnson calculate flight paths?
106578.e: From 1953 she worked at the Langley Research Center in Virginia, at first for the predecessor organisation NACA. There she did calculations for aircraft and later for space flights.
106578.m: Katherine Johnson did calculations for NASA.

106579.q: What was Katherine Johnson’s job called when she started her work?
a: Computer, meaning a person who calculates
106579.e: Before there were powerful electronic calculating machines, people did the many calculations by hand. They were called “computers”.
106579.m: Katherine Johnson started out as a human computer.

106580.q: What did Katherine Johnson mainly use for her calculations at the start of her work?
106580.e: In the 1950s there were hardly any electronic calculating machines. Johnson calculated flight paths, for example for Alan Shepard’s first space flight in 1961, with paper, pencil and mechanical calculating aids.
106580.m: Katherine Johnson calculated flight paths by hand.

106581.q: Which astronaut wanted Katherine Johnson to check the computer calculations before his orbit of the Earth in 1962?
106581.e: He did not yet fully trust the new electronic computers. Only after Johnson had confirmed the numbers by hand was he ready to fly.
106581.m: John Glenn trusted Katherine Johnson’s calculations.

106582.q: Which famous mission did Katherine Johnson help with calculations in 1969?
106582.e: She worked on the trajectory calculations for the first crewed Moon landing. This included how the lunar module would find its way back to the spacecraft.
106582.m: Katherine Johnson did calculations for Apollo 11.

106583.q: What is the 2016 film about Katherine Johnson and her colleagues called?
106583.e: The film tells the story of African American women mathematicians at NASA. It also shows how they had to work under racial segregation.
106583.m: The film “Hidden Figures” tells Katherine Johnson’s story.

106584.q: Which high honour did President Barack Obama present to Katherine Johnson in 2015?
106584.e: The Presidential Medal of Freedom is one of the highest civilian honours in the USA. Johnson was 97 years old at the time.
106584.m: Katherine Johnson received the Medal of Freedom in 2015.

106585.q: How old was Katherine Johnson when she died?
106585.e: She was born in 1918 and died in February 2020. A NASA research building is named after her today.
106585.m: Katherine Johnson lived to the age of 101.

106586.q: Which country does the scientist Tu Youyou come from?
106586.e: Tu Youyou was born in the city of Ningbo in 1930. She studied pharmacy and researched medicinal plants used in her country’s traditional medicine.
106586.m: Tu Youyou is a Chinese pharmacologist.

106587.q: Against which disease did Tu Youyou discover an effective medicine?
106587.e: The disease is spread by mosquitoes and kills hundreds of thousands of people every year. Her drug has saved millions of lives.
106587.m: Tu Youyou’s drug helps against malaria.

106588.q: What is the drug that Tu Youyou discovered called?
106588.e: The substance was obtained from a medicinal plant in the 1970s. It kills the pathogens in the blood very quickly.

106589.q: From which plant did Tu Youyou obtain her drug?
106589.e: The plant’s Latin name is Artemisia annua, and it had long been used in China against fever.
106589.m: The drug comes from sweet wormwood.

106590.q: Where did Tu Youyou find the crucial clue for the right way to make her drug?
a: In a Chinese book of medicines around 1,600 years old
106590.e: In the 4th century, the scholar Ge Hong described a special way of preparing the plant. This clue led Tu to a new method.
106590.m: An ancient book of medicines put Tu Youyou on the right track.

106591.q: Why was boiling the plant a problem at first in Tu Youyou’s research?
a: The heat destroyed the active substance
106591.e: At high temperatures the effect was lost. By extracting it at a low temperature, she achieved the breakthrough.
106591.m: Tu Youyou extracted her drug at a low temperature.

106592.q: In which year did Tu Youyou receive the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine?
106592.e: She shared the prize with two researchers who had developed a medicine against worm diseases. She was the first Chinese woman to win a Nobel Prize in science.
106592.m: Tu Youyou received the Nobel Prize in 2015.

106593.q: What did Tu Youyou do before her drug was tested on sick people?
a: She tested it on herself first
She only gave it to animals in a zoo
106593.e: She wanted to be sure that the substance was not dangerous for humans. So she volunteered to take it together with colleagues.
106593.m: Tu Youyou tested her medicine on her own body first.

106594.q: In which subject did Chien-Shiung Wu do research?
106594.e: Chien-Shiung Wu was an expert in experiments with radioactive atomic nuclei. She was considered one of the most precise experimental physicists of her time.

106595.q: In which country was Chien-Shiung Wu born in 1912?
106595.e: She grew up near Shanghai. In 1936 she moved to the USA to study and spent the rest of her life there.

106596.q: Which secret project during the Second World War did Chien-Shiung Wu work on?
106596.e: In this project the USA built the first atomic bomb. Wu worked on the enrichment of uranium.
106596.m: Chien-Shiung Wu took part in the Manhattan Project.

106597.q: What did Chien-Shiung Wu work with in her experiments?
106597.e: Wu studied how radioactive atomic nuclei decay. Her most famous experiment of 1956/57 changed the picture of physics.
106597.m: Chien-Shiung Wu studied radioactive atomic nuclei.

106598.q: What was Chien-Shiung Wu particularly known for among her colleagues?
106598.e: Wu planned and measured extremely carefully. That is why other researchers relied on her results.
106598.m: Chien-Shiung Wu was a very precise experimental physicist.

106599.q: Why is it still criticised today that Chien-Shiung Wu did not receive a Nobel Prize?
a: She proved the theory, but only the two theorists were honoured
She had done no research at all
She did not want to accept the prize
There was no Nobel Prize at that time
106599.e: In 1957 Tsung-Dao Lee and Chen Ning Yang received the Nobel Prize in Physics for their idea. Wu had proved it in the laboratory but got nothing.
106599.m: Wu proved a Nobel Prize theory but did not receive the prize.

106600.q: What nickname did Chien-Shiung Wu get because of her importance?
106600.e: Colleagues admired her extremely careful measurements. The nickname honoured her as a leading physicist.
106600.m: Chien-Shiung Wu was called the First Lady of Physics.

106601.q: Which important prize did Chien-Shiung Wu receive in 1978 as the very first person in physics?
106601.e: The Wolf Prize is awarded in Israel and is considered one of the highest honours after the Nobel Prize. In physics it went to Wu first.
106601.m: Wu was the first to receive the Wolf Prize in Physics.

106602.q: Why did Maria Skłodowska, who later became Marie Curie, go to Paris to study?
a: Women were not allowed to go to university in her home country, Poland
Paris was the cheapest city in Europe
She wanted to become a painter there
106602.e: In her home country women were not allowed to go to university at that time. In Paris she was finally able to start studying in 1891.
106602.m: Marie Curie went to Paris to study because women in Poland were not allowed to.

106603.q: At which Paris university did Marie Curie study?
106603.e: Unlike in her home country, women could study there. Marie Curie finished her physics degree in 1893 as the best in her year.
106603.m: Marie Curie studied at the Sorbonne.

106604.q: In what kind of room did Marie and Pierre Curie discover their new elements in 1898?
106604.e: The school where Pierre taught only gave them an old shed. In winter it was freezing cold there, and in summer it was hot.
106604.m: The Curies did their research in Paris in a simple shed.

106605.q: Which research institute was built for Marie Curie in Paris and bears her name today?
106605.e: The institute was planned from 1909 and finished shortly before the First World War. Marie Curie ran the physics and chemistry department there; today it is called the Curie Institute.
106605.m: The Radium Institute in Paris was built for Marie Curie.

106606.q: Which term did Marie Curie introduce for the radiation given off by certain substances?
106606.e: The word comes from the Latin “radius”, meaning ray. It describes the fact that certain substances give off radiation by themselves.
106606.m: Marie Curie coined the word radioactivity.

106607.q: What happened in 1911 when Marie Curie applied for a seat in the French Academy of Sciences?
a: She narrowly failed to be elected
106607.e: Many members did not want a woman in the Academy. A male physicist was elected instead, even though Curie was internationally famous.
106607.m: The Academy in Paris narrowly rejected Marie Curie in 1911.

106608.q: How did Marie and Pierre Curie spend their honeymoon after their wedding?
a: On a cycling tour through France
On a voyage by ship to America
On a train journey to Italy
In a hotel in the Alps
106608.e: The two got married in Paris in 1895. For their wedding they bought themselves bicycles and went on a cycling tour through France.
106608.m: Marie and Pierre Curie went on a honeymoon by bicycle.

106609.q: In 1894 in Paris, after physics, in which subject did Marie Curie complete a second degree?
106609.e: One year after her first degree, she also passed this exam very well. This gave her two science diplomas.
106609.m: Marie Curie also studied mathematics in Paris.

106610.q: On which continent did Jane Goodall observe wild chimpanzees?
106610.e: Jane Goodall did her research in Gombe Stream National Park in Tanzania. Wild chimpanzees only live in Africa.
106610.m: Jane Goodall studied chimpanzees in Africa.

106611.q: What did Jane Goodall observe in chimpanzees that people had previously thought only humans could do?
a: They build houses out of stone
106611.e: In 1960 Goodall saw a chimpanzee fishing termites out of their nest with a blade of grass. This changed the picture of humans and animals.

106612.e: Jane Goodall studied how chimpanzees live and behave. This science is called animal behaviour research.
106612.m: Jane Goodall was an animal behaviour scientist.

106613.q: How did Jane Goodall win the trust of the wild chimpanzees?
a: With lots of patience and daily observation
106613.e: At first the animals ran away from her. Because she stayed calmly nearby day after day, the chimpanzees got used to her after months.
106613.m: Patience was Jane Goodall’s most important tool.

106614.q: What did Jane Goodall observe about the diet of chimpanzees that surprised many people?
a: They also hunt and eat meat
106614.e: For a long time chimpanzees were thought to eat only plants. Goodall saw them hunting other monkeys together and sharing the meat.
106614.m: Chimpanzees also hunt and eat meat.

106616.q: Which honour did Jane Goodall receive from the United Nations in 2002?
a: She became a UN Messenger of Peace
She got a seat on the Security Council
106616.e: As a Messenger of Peace she campaigned worldwide for the protection of animals and the environment. Even in old age she travelled for this almost all year round.
106616.m: Jane Goodall was a UN Messenger of Peace.

106617.q: What is special about the chimpanzee research in Gombe?
a: It is one of the longest field studies of wild animals
It only takes place in a laboratory
It is only done with robots
106617.e: For decades the same chimpanzee families have been observed there over many generations. This means their life stories are known especially well.
106617.m: The Gombe study is one of the longest animal studies in the world.

106618.q: Where does the right atrium pass its blood on to?
106618.e: The right atrium contracts and pushes the blood through a valve into the right ventricle below it.
106618.m: Each atrium passes its blood to the ventricle on the same side.

106619.q: What is the technical term for one of the two upper chambers of the heart?
106619.e: In technical language, an upper chamber of the heart is called an atrium, the Latin word for entrance hall. Doctors speak of the right and left atrium.
106619.m: An upper chamber of the heart is called an atrium.

106620.q: Why do the atria have thinner muscle walls than the ventricles?
a: They only push the blood into the nearby ventricle.
They contain no blood at all.
106620.e: The atria only have to move the blood a short distance into the ventricles. This needs little force and so little muscle.
106620.m: The atria need little force and so have thin walls.

106621.q: What is the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder, in which the atria twitch irregularly, called?
106621.e: In atrial fibrillation, the atria no longer contract in an orderly way. It is the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder, especially in older people.
106621.m: Atrial fibrillation is the most common lasting heart rhythm disorder.

106622.q: Why does only a little blood flow through the lungs of an unborn baby?
a: Because it does not breathe yet and gets oxygen through the umbilical cord
Because it has no lungs yet
Because its heart does not beat yet
106622.e: Before birth, the baby gets oxygen through the umbilical cord. That is why most of the blood bypasses the lungs, partly through an opening between the atria.
106622.m: Before birth, most of the blood bypasses the lungs.

106624.q: Roughly how much blood does one ventricle of an adult pump out per heartbeat at rest?
106624.e: This stroke volume is around 70 millilitres at rest, which is about as much as five tablespoons. During sport it can rise a lot.
106624.m: Each ventricle pumps about 70 millilitres of blood per heartbeat.

106625.q: What is the sac of connective tissue that surrounds the whole heart called?
106625.e: The pericardium surrounds the heart like a cover. A thin layer of fluid inside it lets the heart glide smoothly as it beats.
106625.m: The pericardium protects the heart and lets it beat smoothly.

106626.q: How many valves does the human heart have?
106626.e: There are two valves between the atria and the ventricles and two at the exits of the ventricles. Together that makes four.

106627.q: What do you mainly hear when listening to the heart with a stethoscope?
a: The lungs rushing inside the heart
106627.e: The typical heart sounds are made when the heart valves close. In this way doctors can hear whether the valves are working properly.
106627.m: Heart sounds are made when the heart valves close.

106628.q: In which direction do the valves between atrium and ventricle let the blood flow?
a: From the atrium into the ventricle
From the ventricle into the atrium
Not at all, they are always shut
106628.e: The atria collect the blood and pass it on to the ventricles. The valves between them only let it through in this direction.
106628.m: Blood flows from the atrium into the ventricle.

106630.q: What makes the heart valves open and close?
a: Their own muscles in the valves
106630.e: Heart valves move without any force of their own. When blood pushes from one side they open, and when it pushes back they shut like a door in the wind.
106630.m: Blood pressure opens and closes the heart valves.

106631.q: What stops the flap valves from flipping back into the atria when the ventricles contract?
106631.e: Fine tendon cords connect the flaps to small muscles in the wall of the ventricle. They hold the flaps in place like the lines of a parachute.
106631.m: Tendon cords hold the flap valves in position.

106633.q: What is the curved section of the aorta just above the heart called?
106633.e: The aorta first rises upwards and then bends backwards and downwards in an arch. The arteries for the head and arms branch off from the aortic arch.
106633.m: The aortic arch lies just above the heart.

106634.q: Which vessels are the first to branch off the aorta and supply the heart muscle itself?
106634.e: The coronary arteries branch off just after the aortic valve. They lie around the heart like a crown and supply it with oxygen.
106634.m: The coronary arteries supply the heart muscle with blood.

106635.q: What kind of blood flows in the aorta?
106635.e: The blood in the aorta comes straight from the heart after it has picked up fresh oxygen in the lungs. That is why it is rich in oxygen.
106635.m: Oxygen-rich blood flows in the aorta.

106636.q: Why is the aorta the largest artery in the body?
a: All the blood from the left ventricle flows through it
It brings blood back to the heart
It carries air to the lungs
106636.e: The left ventricle pumps the oxygen-rich blood into the aorta. All the arteries of the body’s circulation branch off from it.
106636.m: The aorta is the largest artery in the body.

106637.q: How many venae cavae lead into the heart?
106637.e: There is a superior (upper) and an inferior (lower) vena cava. Both bring blood from the body to the heart.
106637.m: An upper and a lower vena cava lead to the heart.

106638.q: Which chamber of the heart do the venae cavae lead into?
106638.e: Both venae cavae end in the right atrium. That is where the blood’s journey to the lungs begins.
106638.m: The venae cavae lead into the right atrium.

106639.q: From which parts of the body does the superior vena cava collect blood?
a: From the head, neck and arms
106639.e: The superior vena cava brings the blood back from the upper half of the body. This includes the head, neck and arms.
106639.m: The superior vena cava brings blood back from the head and arms.

106640.q: From which areas of the body does the blood in the inferior vena cava come?
106640.e: The inferior vena cava collects the blood from the lower body. It runs up next to the spine to the heart.
106640.m: The inferior vena cava brings blood back from the legs and abdomen.

106641.q: What kind of blood do the venae cavae carry?
106641.e: The blood has given up its oxygen to the organs before it reaches the venae cavae. That is why it is low in oxygen and darker.
106641.m: Used, oxygen-poor blood flows in the venae cavae.

106642.q: Which is the largest vein in the human body?
106642.e: The inferior vena cava has the largest diameter of all veins. It carries the blood of the whole lower half of the body.
106642.m: The inferior vena cava is the largest vein in the body.

106643.q: Where do the venae cavae take the blood?
106643.e: The superior and inferior venae cavae collect the blood from the body and take it back to the heart.
106643.m: The venae cavae take the blood back to the heart.

106644.q: What is the pulmonary circulation also called?
106644.e: The pulmonary circulation only goes from the heart to the lungs and back. Because the route is short, it is called the small circulation.
106644.m: The pulmonary circulation is the small circulation.

106645.q: In which chamber of the heart does the pulmonary circulation begin?
106645.e: The right ventricle pumps the oxygen-poor blood towards the lungs. That is where the pulmonary circulation begins.
106645.m: The pulmonary circulation begins in the right ventricle.

106646.q: Where does the pulmonary circulation end?
106646.e: The fresh blood flows from the lungs back to the heart and reaches the left atrium there. This closes the small circulation.
106646.m: The pulmonary circulation ends in the left atrium.

106647.q: How does blood pressure in the pulmonary circulation compare with the body’s circulation?
106647.e: The lungs are close to the heart, and the delicate air sacs cannot cope with high pressure. That is why the pressure in the pulmonary circulation is much lower.
106647.m: Blood pressure is low in the pulmonary circulation.

106648.q: Which blood vessels bring the blood from the lungs back to the heart?
106648.e: After the exchange of gases, the pulmonary veins collect the fresh blood. They take it back to the heart.
106648.m: The pulmonary veins bring fresh blood from the lungs to the heart.

106649.q: What is the body’s circulation (systemic circulation) also called?
106649.e: The body’s circulation supplies the whole body from head to toe. Because it reaches so far, it is called the large circulation.
106649.m: The body’s circulation is the large circulation.

106650.q: In which chamber of the heart does the body’s circulation begin?
106650.e: The left ventricle pumps the oxygen-rich blood into the body. From there it spreads to all the organs.
106650.m: The body’s circulation begins in the left ventricle.

106651.q: What happens to the ventricles during systole?
a: They contract and pump blood out.
106651.e: During systole, the muscles of the ventricles contract. This pushes the blood into the large arteries.
106651.m: In systole, the ventricles pump the blood out.

106652.q: Where do the ventricles pump the blood during systole?
a: Into the large arteries such as the aorta
106652.e: The ventricles contract and push the blood into the large arteries. Valves stop it from flowing back into the atria.
106652.m: In systole, the blood flows into the arteries.

106653.q: What does the Greek word “systole” literally mean?
106653.e: Systole comes from Greek and means contraction. That is exactly what the heart muscle does in this phase.

106654.q: What happens to the ventricles during diastole?
a: They relax and fill with blood.
They push blood into the aorta.
106654.e: Diastole is the phase of relaxing and filling. The muscles of the ventricles relax, and blood flows in from the atria.
106654.m: In diastole, the ventricles relax and fill.

106655.q: Where does the blood flow into the ventricles from while they relax in diastole?
106655.e: During diastole, the flap valves open. So blood flows from the atria into the ventricles.
106655.m: In diastole, blood flows from the atria into the ventricles.

106656.q: What is the phase called in which the ventricles contract and push blood out?
106656.e: In systole, the ventricles contract and pump blood into the arteries. In diastole, they relax and fill again.
106656.m: Systole means pumping, diastole means relaxing and filling.

106657.q: Which reading when measuring blood pressure belongs to diastole?
106657.e: In 120 over 80, the 80 is the diastolic reading. It shows the pressure in the arteries while the heart relaxes.
